entries.b20cb81c3838fa3573df666adec35efb452b1d9f: <div sID="gen10224" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="39" osisID="Job.39" sID="Job.39"/> <div eID="gen10224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10225" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10226" type="x-p"/> God proceeds here to show Job what little reason he had to charge him with unkindness who was so compassionate to the inferior creatures and took such a tender care of them, or to boast of himself, and his own good deeds before God, which were nothing to the divine mercies. He shows him also what great reason he had to be humble who knew so little of the nature of the creatures about him and had so little influence upon them, and to submit to that God on whom they all depend. He discourses particularly, I. Concerning the wild goats and hinds, <reference osisRef="Job.39.1-Job.39.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. Concerning the wild ass, <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.39.8">ver. 5-8</reference>. III. Concerning the unicorn, <reference osisRef="Job.39.9-Job.39.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. IV. Concerning the peacock, <reference osisRef="Job.39.13">ver. 13</reference>. V. Concerning the ostrich, <reference osisRef="Job.39.13-Job.39.18">ver. 13-18</reference>. VI. Concerning the horse, <reference osisRef="Job.39.19-Job.39.25">ver. 19-25</reference>. VII. Concerning the hawk and the eagle, <reference osisRef="Job.39.26-Job.39.30">ver. 26-30</reference>.
entries.bc2994362dc745c98023c32b0decd54bc69e2a8e: <div eID="gen10226" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10225" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Man's Ignorance of the Animal Creation; Description of the Wild Goat, Hind, Wild Ass, and Unicorn. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10227" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? <hi type="italic">or</hi> canst thou mark when the hinds do calve? <hi type="super">2</hi> Canst thou number the months <hi type="italic">that</hi> they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? <hi type="super">3</hi> They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones, they cast out their sorrows. <hi type="super">4</hi> Their young ones are in good liking, they grow up with corn; they go forth, and return not unto them. 5 Who hath sent out the wild ass free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? <hi type="super">6</hi> Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the barren land his dwellings. <hi type="super">7</hi> He scorneth the multitude of the city, neither regardeth he the crying of the driver. <hi type="super">8</hi> The range of the mountains <hi type="italic">is</hi> his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing. <hi type="super">9</hi> Will the unicorn be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib? <hi type="super">10</hi> Canst thou bind the unicorn with his band in the furrow? or will he harrow the valleys after thee? <hi type="super">11</hi> Wilt thou trust him, because his strength <hi type="italic">is</hi> great? or wilt thou leave thy labour to him? <hi type="super">12</hi> Wilt thou believe him, that he will bring home thy seed, and gather <hi type="italic">it into</hi> thy barn? <div eID="gen10227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10228" type="x-p"/> God here shows Job what little acquaintance he had with the untamed creatures that run wild in the deserts and live at large, but are the care of the divine Providence. As, <div eID="gen10228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10229" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">wild goats</hi> and the <hi type="italic">hinds.</hi> That which is taken notice of concerning them is the bringing forth and bringing up of their young ones. For, as every individual is fed, so every species of animals is preserved, by the care of the divine Providence, and, for aught we know, none extinct to this day. Observe here, 1. Concerning the production of their young, (1.) Man is wholly ignorant of the time when they bring forth, <reference osisRef="Job.39.1-Job.39.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Shall we pretend to tell what is in the womb of Providence, or what a day will bring forth, who know not the time of the pregnancy of a hind or a wild goat? (2.) Though they bring forth their young with a great deal of difficulty and sorrow, and have no assistance from man, yet, by the good providence of God, their young ones are safely produced, and their sorrows cast out and forgotten, <reference osisRef="Job.39.3">v. 3</reference>. Some think it is intimated (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.9">Ps. xxix. 9</reference>) that God by thunder helps the hinds in calving. Let it be observed, for the comfort of women in labour, that God helps even the hinds to bring forth their young; and shall he not much more succour them, and save them in child-bearing, who are his children in covenant with him? 2. Concerning the growth of their young, (<reference osisRef="Job.39.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They are in good liking;</hi> though they are brought forth in sorrow, after their dams have suckled them awhile they shift for themselves in the corn-fields, and are no more burdensome to them, which is an example to children, when they have grown up, not to be always hanging upon their parents and craving from them, but to put forth themselves to get their own livelihood and to requite their parents. <div eID="gen10229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10230" type="x-p"/> II. The <hi type="italic">wild ass,</hi> a creature we frequently read of in Scripture, some say untameable. Man is said to be born as the wild ass's colt, so hard to be governed. Two things Providence has allotted to the wild ass:—1. An unbounded liberty (<reference osisRef="Job.39.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who</hi> but God <hi type="italic">has sent out the wild ass free?</hi> He has given a disposition to it, and therefore a dispensation for it. The tame ass is bound to labour; the wild ass has no bonds on him. Note, Freedom from service, and liberty to range at pleasure, are but the privileges of a wild ass. It is a pity that any of the children of men should covet such a liberty, or value themselves on it. It is better to labour and be good for something than ramble and be good for nothing. But if, among men, Providence sets some at liberty and suffers them to live at ease, while others are doomed to servitude, we must not marvel at the matter: it is so among the brute-creatures. 2. An unenclosed lodging (<reference osisRef="Job.39.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whose house I have made the wilderness,</hi> where he has room enough to traverse his ways, and snuff up the wind at his pleasure, as the wild ass is said to do (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jer. ii. 24</reference>), as if he had to live upon the air, for it is <hi type="italic">the barren land</hi> that is <hi type="italic">his dwelling.</hi> Observe, The tame ass, that labours, and is serviceable to man, has his master's crib to go to both for shelter and food, and lives in a fruitful land: but the wild ass, that will have his liberty, must have it in a barren land. He that will not labour, let him not eat. He that will shall eat the labour of his hands, and have also to give to him that needs. Jacob, the shepherd, has good red pottage to spare, when Esau, a sportsman, is ready to perish for hunger. A further description of the liberty and livelihood of the wild ass we have, <reference osisRef="Job.39.7-Job.39.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. (1.) He has no owner, nor will he be in subjection: <hi type="italic">He scorns the multitude of the city.</hi> If they attempt to take him, and in order to that surround him with a multitude, he will soon get clear of them, and <hi type="italic">the crying of the driver</hi> is nothing to him. He laughs at those that live in the tumult and bustle of cities (so bishop Patrick), thinking himself happier in the wilderness; and opinion is the rate of things. (2.) Having no owner, he has no feeder, nor is any provision made for him, but he must shift for himself: <hi type="italic">The range of the mountains is his pasture,</hi> and a bare pasture it is; there he <hi type="italic">searches after here and there a green thing,</hi> as he can find it and pick it up; whereas the labouring asses have green things in plenty, without their searching for them. From the untameableness of this and other creatures we may infer how unfit we are to give law to Providence, who cannot give law even to a wild ass's colt. <div eID="gen10230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10231" type="x-p"/> III. The unicorn—<hi type="italic">rhem,</hi> a strong creature (<reference osisRef="Num.23.22">Num. xxiii. 22</reference>), a stately proud creature, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>. He is able to serve, but not willing; and God here challenges Job to force him to it. Job expected every thing should be just as he would have it. "Since thou dost pretend" (says God) "to bring every thing beneath thy sway, begin with the unicorn, and try thy skill upon him. Now that thy oxen and asses are all gone, try whether he will be willing to serve thee in their stead (<reference osisRef="Job.39.9">v. 9</reference>) and whether he will be content with the provision thou usedst to make for them: <hi type="italic">Will he abide by thy crib?</hi> No;" 1. "Thou canst not tame him, nor <hi type="italic">bind him with his band,</hi> nor set him to <hi type="italic">draw the harrow,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.39.10">v. 10</reference>. There are creatures that are willing to serve man, that seem to take a pleasure in serving him, and to have a love for their masters; but there are such as will never be brought to serve him, which is the effect of sin. Man has revolted from his subjection to his Maker, and is therefore justly punished with the revolt of the inferior creatures from their subjection to him; and yet, as an instance of God's good-will to man, there are some that are still serviceable to him. Though the wild bull (which some think is meant here by the unicorn) will not serve him, nor submit to his hand in the furrows, yet there are tame bullocks that will, and other animals that are not <hi type="italic">feræ naturæ—of a wild nature,</hi> in whom man may have a property, for whom he provides, and to whose service he is entitled. <hi type="italic">Lord, what is man, that thou art thus mindful of him?</hi> 2. "Thou darest not trust him; though <hi type="italic">his strength is great,</hi> yet thou wilt not <hi type="italic">leave thy labour to him,</hi> as thou dost with thy asses or oxen, which a little child may lead or drive, leaving to them all the pains. Thou wilt never depend upon the wild bull, as likely to come to thy harvest-work, much less to go through it, to <hi type="italic">bring home thy seed and gather it into thy barn,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.39.11-Job.39.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. And, because he will not serve about the corn, he is not so well fed as the tame ox, whose mouth was not to be muzzled in treading out the corn; but <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he will not draw the plough, because he that made him never designed him for it. A disposition to labour is as much the gift of God as an ability for it; and it is a great mercy if, where God gives strength for service, he gives a heart; it is what we should pray for, and reason ourselves into, which the brutes cannot do; for, as among beasts, so among men, those may justly be reckoned wild and abandoned to the deserts who have no mind either to take pains or to do good.
entries.586d54e02ed3bcaf7d0bad4772953cb8ad037e75: <div eID="gen10231" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Description of the Peacock and Ostrich. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> <hi type="italic">Gavest thou</hi> the goodly wings unto the peacocks? or wings and feathers unto the ostrich? <hi type="super">14</hi> Which leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in dust, <hi type="super">15</hi> And forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may break them. <hi type="super">16</hi> She is hardened against her young ones, as though <hi type="italic">they were</hi> not hers: her labour is in vain without fear; <hi type="super">17</hi> Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding. <hi type="super">18</hi> What time she lifteth up herself on high, she scorneth the horse and his rider. <div eID="gen10232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10233" type="x-p"/> The ostrich is a wonderful animal, a very large bird, but it never flies. Some have called it <hi type="italic">a winged camel.</hi> God here gives an account of it, and observes, <div eID="gen10233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10234" type="x-p"/> I. Something that it has in common with the peacock, that is, beautiful feathers <reference osisRef="Job.39.13">(v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gavest thou proud wings unto the peacocks?</hi> so some read it. Fine feathers make proud birds. The peacock is an emblem of pride; when he struts, and shows his fine feathers, Solomon in all his glory is not arrayed like him. The ostrich too has goodly feathers, and yet is a foolish bird; for wisdom does not always go along with beauty and gaiety. Other birds do not envy the peacock or the ostrich their gaudy colours, nor complain for want of them; why then should we repine if we see others wear better clothes than we can afford to wear? God gives his gifts variously, and those gifts are not always the most valuable that make the finest show. Who would not rather have the voice of the nightingale than the tail of the peacock, the eye of the eagle and her soaring wing, and the natural affection of the stork, than the beautiful wings and feathers of the ostrich, which can never rise above the earth, and is without natural affection? <div eID="gen10234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10235" type="x-p"/> II. Something that is peculiar to itself, <div eID="gen10235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10236" type="x-p"/> 1. Carelessness of her young. It is well that this is peculiar to herself, for it is a very bad character. Observe, (1.) How she exposes her eggs; she does not retire to some private place, and make a nest there, as the sparrows and swallows do (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.3">Ps. lxxxiv. 3</reference>), and there lay eggs and hatch her young. Most birds, as well as other animals, are strangely guided by natural instinct in providing for the preservation of their young. But the ostrich is a monster in nature, for she drops her eggs any where upon the ground and takes no care to hatch them. If the sand and the sun will hatch them, well and good; they may for her, for she will not warm them, <reference osisRef="Job.39.14">v. 14</reference>. Nay, she takes no care to preserve them: <hi type="italic">The foot</hi> of the traveller <hi type="italic">may crush them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the wild beast break them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.15">v. 15</reference>. But how then are any young ones brought forth, and whence is it that the species has not perished? We must suppose either that God, by a special providence, with the heat of the sun and the sand (so some think), hatches the neglected eggs of the ostrich, as he feeds the neglected young ones of the raven, or that, though the ostrich <hi type="italic">often</hi> leaves her eggs thus, yet not <hi type="italic">always.</hi> (2.) The reason why she does thus expose her eggs. It is, [1.] For want of natural affection (<reference osisRef="Job.39.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">She is hardened against her young ones.</hi> To be hardened against any is unamiable, even in a brute-creature, much more in a rational creature that boasts of humanity, especially to be hardened against young ones, that cannot help themselves and therefore merit compassion, that give no provocation and therefore merit no hard usage: but it is worst of all for her to be hardened against her own young ones, as though they were not hers, whereas really they are parts of herself. Her labour in laying her eggs is in vain and all lost, because she has not that fear and tender concern for them that she should have. Those are most likely to lose their labour that are least in fear of losing it. [2.] For want of wisdom (<reference osisRef="Job.39.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">God has deprived her of wisdom.</hi> This intimates that the art which other animals have to nourish and preserve their young is God's gift, and that, where it exists not, God denies it, that by the folly of the ostrich, as well as by the wisdom of the ant, we may learn to be wise; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As careless as the ostrich is of her eggs so careless many people are of their own souls; they make no provision for them, no proper nest in which they may be safe, leave them exposed to Satan and his temptations, which is a certain evidence that they are deprived of wisdom. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> So careless are many parents of their children; some of their bodies, not providing for their own house, their own bowels, and therefore worse than infidels, and as bad as the ostrich; but many more are thus careless of their children's souls, take no care of their education, send them abroad into the world untaught, unarmed, forgetting what corruption there is in the world through lust, which will certainly crush them. Thus their labour in rearing them comes to be in vain; it were better for their country that they had never been born. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> So careless are too many ministers of their people, with whom they should reside; but they leave them in the earth, and forget how busy Satan is to sow tares while men sleep. They overlook those whom they should oversee, and are really hardened against them. <div eID="gen10236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10237" type="x-p"/> 2. Care of herself. She leaves her eggs in danger, but, if she herself be in danger, no creature shall strive more to get out of the way of it than the ostrich, <reference osisRef="Job.39.18">v. 18</reference>. Then she lifts up her wings on high (the strength of which then stands her in better stead than their beauty), and, with the help of them, runs so fast that a horseman at full speed cannot overtake her: <hi type="italic">She scorneth the horse and his rider.</hi> Those that are least under the law of natural affection often contend most for the law of self-preservation. Let not the rider be proud of the swiftness of his horse when such an animal as the ostrich shall out-run him.
entries.a16416631e47c75b972629690ed77bb84d03fd93: <div eID="gen10237" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Description of the War-Horse. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with thunder? <hi type="super">20</hi> Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? the glory of his nostrils <hi type="italic">is</hi> terrible. 21 He paweth in the valley, and rejoiceth in <hi type="italic">his</hi> strength: he goeth on to meet the armed men. <hi type="super">22</hi> He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword. <hi type="super">23</hi> The quiver rattleth against him, the glittering spear and the shield. <hi type="super">24</hi> He swalloweth the ground with fierceness and rage: neither believeth he that <hi type="italic">it is</hi> the sound of the trumpet. <hi type="super">25</hi> He saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha; and he smelleth the battle afar off, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting. <div eID="gen10238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10239" type="x-p"/> God, having displayed his own power in those creatures that are strong and despise man, here shows it in one scarcely inferior to any of them in strength, and yet very tame and serviceable to man, and that is the horse, especially <hi type="italic">the horse that is prepared against the day of battle</hi> and is serviceable to man at a time when he has more than ordinary occasion for his service. It seems, there was, in Job's country, a noble generous breed of horses. Job, it is probable, kept many, though they are not mentioned among his possessions, cattle for use in husbandry being there valued more than those for state and war, which alone horses were then reserved for, and they were not then put to such mean services as with us they are commonly put to. Concerning the great horse, that stately beast, it is here observed, 1. That he has a great deal of strength and spirit (<reference osisRef="Job.39.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hast thou given the horse strength?</hi> He uses his strength for man, but has it not from him: God gave it to him, who is the fountain of all the powers of nature, and yet he himself <hi type="italic">delights not in the strength of the horse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.10">Ps. cxlvii. 10</reference>), but has told us that <hi type="italic">a horse is a vain thing for safety,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.33.17">Ps. xxxiii. 17</reference>. For running, drawing, and carrying, no creature that is ordinarily in the service of man has so much strength as the horse has, nor is of so stout and bold a spirit, not to be made afraid as a grasshopper, but daring and forward to face danger. It is a mercy to man to have such a servant, which, though very strong, submits to the management of a child, and rebels not against his owner. But let not the strength of a horse be trusted to, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.3 Ps.20.7 ">Hos. xiv. 3; Ps. xx. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1 Isa.31.3">Isa. xxxi. 1, 3</reference>. 2. That his neck and nostrils look great. His neck is <hi type="italic">clothed with thunder,</hi> with a large and flowing mane, which makes him formidable and is an ornament to him. <hi type="italic">The glory of his nostrils,</hi> when he snorts, flings up his head, and throws foam about, <hi type="italic">is terrible,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">v. 20</reference>. Perhaps there might be at that time, and in that country, a more stately breed of horses than any we have now. 3. That he is very fierce and furious in battle, and charges with an undaunted courage, though he pushes on in imminent danger of his life. (1.) See how frolicsome he is (<reference osisRef="Job.39.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">He paws in the valley,</hi> scarcely knowing what ground he stands upon. He is proud of his strength, and he has much more reason to be so as using his strength in the service of man, and under his direction, than the wild ass that uses it in contempt of man, and in a revolt from him <reference osisRef="Job.39.8">v. 8</reference>. (2.) See how forward he is to engage: <hi type="italic">He goes on to meet the armed men,</hi> animated, not by the goodness of the cause, or the prospect of honour, but only by <hi type="italic">the sound of the trumpet, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting</hi> of the soldiers, which are as bellows to the fire of his innate courage, and make him spring forward with the utmost eagerness, as if he cried, <hi type="italic">Ha! ha!</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.25">v. 25</reference>. How wonderfully are the brute-creatures fitted for and inclined to the services for which they were designed. (3.) See how fearless he is, how he despises death and the most threatening dangers, (<reference osisRef="Job.39.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He mocks at fear,</hi> and makes a jest of it; slash at him with a sword, rattle the quiver, brandish the spear, to drive him back, he will not retreat, but press forward, and even inspires courage into his rider. (4.) See how furious he is. He curvets and prances, and runs on with so much violence and heat against the enemy that one would think he even <hi type="italic">swallowed the ground with fierceness and rage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">v. 24</reference>. High mettle is the praise of a horse rather than of a man, whom fierceness and rage ill become. This description of the war-horse will help to explain that character which is given of presumptuous sinners, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Every one turneth to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.</hi> When a man's heart is fully set in him to do evil, and he is carried on in a wicked way by the violence of inordinate appetites and passions, there is no making him afraid of the wrath of God and the fatal consequences of sin. Let his own conscience set before him the curse of the law, the death that is the wages of sin, and all the terrors of the Almighty in battle-array; he mocks at this fear, and is not affrighted, neither turns he back from the flaming sword of the cherubim. Let ministers lift up their voice like a trumpet, to proclaim the wrath of God against him, <hi type="italic">he believes not that it is the sound of the trumpet,</hi> nor that God and his heralds are in earnest with him; but what will be in the end hereof it is easy to foresee.
entries.d120b3afe371a77ac039d5430f5f968e3c89e053: <div eID="gen10239" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Description of the Hawk and Eagle. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> stretch her wings toward the south? <hi type="super">27</hi> Doth the eagle mount up at thy command, and make her nest on high? <hi type="super">28</hi> She dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the strong place. <hi type="super">29</hi> From thence she seeketh the prey, <hi type="italic">and</hi> her eyes behold afar off. <hi type="super">30</hi> Her young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain <hi type="italic">are,</hi> there <hi type="italic">is</hi> she. <div eID="gen10240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10241" type="x-p"/> The birds of the air are proofs of the wonderful power and providences of God, as well as the beasts of the earth; God here refers particularly to two stately ones:—1. The <hi type="italic">hawk,</hi> a noble bird of great strength and sagacity, and yet a bird of prey, <reference osisRef="Job.39.26">v. 26</reference>. This bird is here taken notice of for her flight, which is swift and strong, and especially for the course she steers <hi type="italic">towards the south,</hi> whither she follows the sun in winter, out of the colder countries in the north, especially when she is to cast her plumes and renew them. This is her wisdom, and it was God that gave her this wisdom, not man. Perhaps the extraordinary wisdom of the hawk's flight after her prey was not used then for men's diversion and recreation, as it has been since. It is a pity that the reclaimed hawk, which is taught to fly at man's command and to make him sport, should at any time be abused to the dishonour of God, since it is from God that she receives that wisdom which makes her flight entertaining and serviceable. 2. The <hi type="italic">eagle,</hi> a royal bird, and yet a bird of prey too, the permission of which, nay, the giving of power to which, may help to reconcile us to the prosperity of oppressors among men. The eagle is here taken notice of, (1.) For the height of her flight. No bird soars so high, has so strong a wind, nor can so well bear the light of the sun. Now, "<hi type="italic">Doth she mount at thy command?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.27">v. 27</reference>. Is it by any strength she has from thee? or dost thou direct her flight? No; it is by the natural power and instinct God has given her that she will soar out of thy sight, much more out of thy call." (2.) For the strength of her nest. Her house is her castle and strong-hold; she makes it <hi type="italic">on high</hi> and <hi type="italic">on the rock, the crag of the rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.39.28">v. 28</reference>), which sets her and her young out of the reach of danger. Secure sinners think themselves as safe in their sins as the eagle in her nest on high, in the <hi type="italic">clefts of the rock; but I will bring thee down thence, saith the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">Jer. xlix. 16</reference>. The higher bad men sit above the resentments of the earth the nearer they ought to think themselves to the vengeance of Heaven. (3.) For her quicksightedness (<reference osisRef="Job.39.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Her eyes behold afar off,</hi> not upwards, but downwards, in quest of her prey. In this she is an emblem of a hypocrite, who, while, in the profession of religion, he seems to rise towards heaven, keeps his eye and heart upon the prey on earth, some temporal advantage, some widow's house or other that he hopes to devour, under pretence of devotion. (4.) For the way she has of maintaining herself and her young. She preys upon living animals, which she seizes and tears to pieces, and thence carries to her young ones, which are taught to <hi type="italic">suck up blood;</hi> they do it by instinct, and know no better; but for men that have reason and conscience to thirst after blood is what could scarcely be believed if there had not been in every age wretched instances of it. She also preys upon the dead bodies of men: <hi type="italic">Where the slain are, there is she,</hi> These birds of prey (in another sense than the horse, <reference osisRef="Job.39.25">v. 25</reference>) <hi type="italic">smell the battle afar off.</hi> Therefore, when a great slaughter is to be made among the enemies of the church, the fowls are invited to <hi type="italic">the supper of the great God, to eat the flesh of kings and captains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18">Rev. xix. 17, 18</reference>. Our Saviour refers to this instinct of the eagle, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">Matt. xxiv. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together.</hi> Every creature will make towards that which is its proper food; for he that provides the creatures their food has implanted in them that inclination. These and many such instances of natural power and sagacity in the inferior creatures, which we cannot account for, oblige us to confess our own weakness and ignorance and to give glory to God as the fountain of all being, power, wisdom, and perfection.  <chapter eID="Job.39"/> <div eID="gen10241" type="x-p"/>

entries.9ff1fa6a12d45cf0f9d87edf7542179eb3d941f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5355"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 39</title> <div sID="gen8035" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.39.1-Job.39.30">Job 39:1-30</reference>.<div eID="gen8035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5355"/>1. Even wild beasts, cut off from all care of man, are cared for by God at their seasons of greatest need. Their instinct comes direct from God and guides them to help themselves in parturition; the very time when the herdsman is most anxious for his herds.<div eID="gen8036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wild goats--</hi>ibex (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.18">Psa 104:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.2">1Sa 24:2</reference>).<div eID="gen8037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8038" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hinds--</hi>fawns; most timid and defenseless animals, yet cared for by God. <div eID="gen8038" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b5b75995071cd6cf3a4ff6b2a85adc121f8b834: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5356"/><div sID="gen8039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5356"/>2. They bring forth with ease and do not need to reckon the months of pregnancy, as the shepherd does in the case of his flocks. <div eID="gen8039" type="x-p"/>
entries.1f0783616de9e5deb55e4113a04b1199a53bffde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5357"/><div sID="gen8040" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5357"/><hi type="bold">3. bow themselves--</hi>in parturition; bend on their knees (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.19">1Sa 4:19</reference>).<div eID="gen8040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring forth--</hi>literally, "cause their young to cleave the womb and break forth."<div eID="gen8041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorrows--</hi>their young ones, the cause of their momentary pains. <div eID="gen8042" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c753fea6a72ec2f994c1afa501e3200a81b18b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5358"/><div sID="gen8043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5358"/><hi type="bold">4. are in good liking--</hi>in good condition, grow up strong.<div eID="gen8043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with corn--</hi>rather, "in the field," without man's care.<div eID="gen8044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return not--</hi>being able to provide for themselves. <div eID="gen8045" type="x-p"/>
entries.be0e5a57074c3ca34ccf685bc67b54f47640169d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5359"/><div sID="gen8046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5359"/><hi type="bold">5. wild ass--</hi>Two different Hebrew words are here used for the same animal, "the ass of the woods" and "the wild ass." (See on <reference osisRef="Job.6.5">Job 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.5">Job 24:5</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jr 2:24</reference>).<div eID="gen8046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loosed the bands--</hi>given its liberty to. Man can rob animals of freedom, but not, as God, give freedom, combined with subordination to fixed laws. <div eID="gen8047" type="x-p"/>
entries.5da9e0cb4d167b898eb1a5968909297963baa9ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5360"/><div sID="gen8048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5360"/><hi type="bold">6. barren--</hi>literally, "salt," that is, unfruitful. (So <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Psa 107:34</reference>, Margin.) <div eID="gen8048" type="x-p"/>
entries.6139ad2ab96af136fd48a34e5b9445b4ee8a179b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5361"/><div sID="gen8049" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5361"/><hi type="bold">7. multitude--</hi>rather, "din"; he sets it at defiance, being far away from it in the freedom of the wilderness.<div eID="gen8049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">driver--</hi>who urges on the tame ass to work. The wild ass is the symbol of uncontrolled freedom in the East; even kings have, therefore, added its name to them. <div eID="gen8050" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a205b47ce37a706088c8fa9461e4fd92bd57f2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5362"/><div sID="gen8051" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5362"/><hi type="bold">8. The range--</hi>literally, "searching," "that which it finds by searching is his pasture." <div eID="gen8051" type="x-p"/>
entries.1cf2a0f3d715937ab2033cb9714f585292c5d863: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5363"/><div sID="gen8052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5363"/><hi type="bold">9. unicorn--</hi>Pliny [Natural History, 8.21], mentions such an animal; its figure is found depicted in the ruins of Persepolis. The Hebrew reem conveys the idea of loftiness and power (compare Ramah; Indian, Ram; Latin, Roma). The rhinoceros was perhaps the original type of the unicorn. The Arab rim is a two-horned animal. Sometimes "unicorn" or reem is a mere poetical symbol or abstraction; but the buffalo is the animal referred to here, from the contrast to the tame ox, used in ploughing (<reference osisRef="Job.39.10">Job 39:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.39.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen8052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abide--</hi>literally, "pass the night."<div eID="gen8053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crib--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen8054" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8f9df7c4ced154a65189a27b6c60796f848c217: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5364"/><div sID="gen8055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5364"/><hi type="bold">10. his band--</hi>fastened to the horns, as its chief strength lies in the head and shoulders.<div eID="gen8055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after thee--</hi>obedient to thee; willing to follow, instead of being goaded on before thee. <div eID="gen8056" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c473680e3aa77ed4e26144b17898f8cb101f816: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5365"/><div sID="gen8057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5365"/><hi type="bold">11. thy labour--</hi>rustic work. <div eID="gen8057" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c941ebad502c6379dd9eb72483c1523bb18ac94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5366"/><div sID="gen8058" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5366"/><hi type="bold">12. believe--</hi>trust.<div eID="gen8058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seed--</hi>produce (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.15">1Sa 8:15</reference>).<div eID="gen8059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into thy barn--</hi>rather, "gather (the contents of) thy threshing-floor" [Maurer]; the corn threshed on it. <div eID="gen8060" type="x-p"/>
entries.d64efd9250852e177420297046e12b4584743fb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5367"/><div sID="gen8061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5367"/><hi type="bold">13. Rather, "the wing of the ostrich hen"--</hi>literally, "the crying bird"; as the Arab name for it means "song"; referring to its night cries (<reference osisRef="Job.30.29">Job 30:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.8">Mi 1:8</reference>) vibrating joyously. "Is it not like the quill and feathers of the pious bird" (the stork)? [Umbreit]. The vibrating, quivering wing, serving for sail and oar at once, is characteristic of the ostrich in full course. Its white and black feathers in the wing and tail are like the stork's. But, unlike that bird, the symbol of parental love in the East, it with seeming want of natural (pious) affection deserts its young. Both birds are poetically called by descriptive, instead of their usual appellative, names. <div eID="gen8061" type="x-p"/>
entries.96b26c2bb798c70933efa62664484f71e21ac275: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5368"/><div sID="gen8062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5368"/>14-15. Yet (unlike the stork) she "leaveth," &c. Hence called by the Arabs "the impious bird." However, the fact is, she lays her eggs with great care and hatches them, as other birds do; but in hot countries the eggs do not need so constant incubation; she therefore often leaves them and sometimes forgets the place on her return. Moreover, the outer eggs, intended for food, she feeds to her young; these eggs, lying separate in the sand, exposed to the sun, gave rise to the idea of her altogether leaving them. God describes her as she seems to man; implying, though she may seem foolishly to neglect her young, yet really she is guided by a sure instinct from God, as much as animals of instincts widely different. <div eID="gen8062" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa16da344f8d67d5188e7cdf6c6bb011869a49c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5369"/><div sID="gen8063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5369"/>16. On a slight noise she often forsakes her eggs, and returns not, as if she were "hardened towards her young."<div eID="gen8063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her labour--</hi>in producing eggs, is in vain, (yet) she has not disquietude (about her young), unlike other birds, who, if one egg and another are taken away, will go on laying till their full number is made up. <div eID="gen8064" type="x-p"/>
entries.731c2b01f06cadbada314636e454d619de607644: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5370"/><div sID="gen8065" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5370"/><hi type="bold">17. wisdom--</hi>such as God gives to other animals, and to man (<reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job 35:11</reference>). The Arab proverb is, "foolish as an ostrich." Yet her very seeming want of wisdom is not without wise design of God, though man cannot see it; just as in the trials of the godly, which seem so unreasonable to Job, there lies hid a wise design. <div eID="gen8065" type="x-p"/>
entries.85e5669fe8e0df2e014cb19df26442041f6cd36b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5371"/><div sID="gen8066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5371"/>18. Notwithstanding her deficiencies, she has distinguishing excellences.<div eID="gen8066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifteth ... herself--</hi>for running; she cannot mount in the air. Gesenius translates: "lashes herself" up to her course by flapping her wings. The old versions favor English Version, and the parallel "scorneth" answers to her proudly "lifting up herself." <div eID="gen8067" type="x-p"/>
entries.815bb52db4dabfdb8e5a71b1859e8efc61c7fccd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5372"/><div sID="gen8068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5372"/>19. The allusion to "the horse" (<reference osisRef="Job.39.18">Job 39:18</reference>), suggests the description of him. Arab poets delight in praising the horse; yet it is not mentioned in the possessions of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.1.3">Job 1:3</reference>; 42:12). It seems to have been at the time chiefly used for war, rather than "domestic purposes."<div eID="gen8068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thunder--</hi>poetically for, "he with arched neck inspires fear as thunder does." Translate, "majesty" [Umbreit]. Rather "the trembling, quivering mane," answering to the "vibrating wing" of the ostrich (see on <reference osisRef="Job.39.13">Job 39:13</reference>) [Maurer]. "Mane" in Greek also is from a root meaning "fear." English Version is more sublime. <div eID="gen8069" type="x-p"/>
entries.e168bb0809d00aedf79f02a5b55d648882beb244: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5373"/><div sID="gen8070" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5373"/><hi type="bold">20. make ... afraid--</hi>rather, "canst thou (as I do) make him spring as the locust?" So in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.4">Joe 2:4</reference>, the comparison is between locusts and war-horses. The heads of the two are so similar that the Italians call the locusts cavaletta, "little horse."<div eID="gen8070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nostrils--</hi>snorting furiously. <div eID="gen8071" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca9088d60c27f13a507bff3ed28d519169c9f7ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5374"/><div sID="gen8072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5374"/><hi type="bold">21. valley--</hi>where the battle is joined.<div eID="gen8072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goeth on--</hi>goeth forth (<reference osisRef="Num.1.3">Nu 1:3</reference>; 21:23). <div eID="gen8073" type="x-p"/>
entries.51297410c857fb86c3ed928540186a606897c2cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5375"/><div sID="gen8074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5375"/><hi type="bold">23. quiver--</hi>for the arrows, which they contain, and which are directed "against him."<div eID="gen8074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glittering spear--</hi>literally, "glittering of the spear," like "lightning of the spear" (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.11">Ha 3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen8075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shield--</hi>rather, "lance." <div eID="gen8076" type="x-p"/>
entries.02dee06c88b54c5a07d4b010f88747b04b80e45d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5376"/><div sID="gen8077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5376"/><hi type="bold">24. swalloweth--</hi>Fretting with impatience, he draws the ground towards him with his hoof, as if he would swallow it. The parallelism shows this to be the sense; not as Maurer, "scours over it."<div eID="gen8077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither believeth--</hi>for joy. Rather, "he will not stand still, when the note of the trumpet (soundeth)." <div eID="gen8078" type="x-p"/>
entries.1312d83ce56aecb2004d2249aebf6b4dc0f47886: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5377"/><div sID="gen8079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5377"/><hi type="bold">25. saith--</hi>poetically applied to his mettlesome neighing, whereby he shows his love of the battle.<div eID="gen8079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smelleth--</hi>snuffeth; discerneth (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.3">Is 11:3</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen8080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thunder--</hi>thundering voice. <div eID="gen8081" type="x-p"/>
entries.0adf4127a5b5b0fa75de58d9b550e00339e19659: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5378"/><div sID="gen8082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5378"/>26. The instinct by which some birds migrate to warmer climes before winter. Rapid flying peculiarly characterizes the whole hawk genus. <div eID="gen8082" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8bfd24828cf91b438f4f0df36f3b84abaa0cbd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5379"/><div sID="gen8083" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5379"/><hi type="bold">27. eagle--</hi>It flies highest of all birds: thence called "the bird of heaven." <div eID="gen8083" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b9df62ede41c658e5298240d0ef2a5ba1f53e09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5380"/><div sID="gen8084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5380"/><hi type="bold">28. abideth--</hi>securely (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference>); it occupies the same abode mostly for life.<div eID="gen8084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crag--</hi>literally, "tooth" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.5">1Sa 14:5</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen8085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong place--</hi>citadel, fastness. <div eID="gen8086" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0f09ebadca017e22427c2d9786e5ae901a69e4f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5381"/><div sID="gen8087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5381"/><hi type="bold">29. seeketh--</hi>is on the lookout for.<div eID="gen8087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold--</hi>The eagle descries its prey at an astonishing distance, by sight, rather than smell. <div eID="gen8088" type="x-p"/>
entries.05bfd14bb5f96416e952edbfae082a7b3df366c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5382"/><div sID="gen8089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5382"/>30. Quoted partly by Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">Mt 24:28</reference>). The food of young eagles is the blood of victims brought by the parent, when they are still too feeble to devour flesh.<div eID="gen8089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">slain--</hi>As the vulture chiefly feeds on carcasses, it is included probably in the eagle genus. <chapter eID="Job.39"/>

entries.c43740650cf3065f273cc57c5ca0082dbc70bb60: <div eID="gen17922" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17923" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17924" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17924" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17923" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17925" type="x-p"/> Several animals described: the wild goats and hinds, <reference osisRef="Job.39.1-Job.39.4">Job 39:1-4</reference>. The wild ass, <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.39.8">Job 39:5-8</reference>. The unicorn, <reference osisRef="Job.39.9-Job.39.12">Job 39:9-12</reference>. The peacock and ostrich, <reference osisRef="Job.39.13-Job.39.18">Job 39:13-18</reference>. The war-horse, <reference osisRef="Job.39.19-Job.39.25">Job 39:19-25</reference>. The hawk, <reference osisRef="Job.39.26">Job 39:26</reference>. And the eagle and her brood, <reference osisRef="Job.39.27-Job.39.30">Job 39:27-30</reference>. <div eID="gen17925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17926" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17927" type="x-p"/> Knowest thou the time - To know time, etc., only, was easy, and has nothing extraordinary in it; but the meaning of these questions is, to know the circumstances, which have something peculiarly expressive of God's providence, and make the questions proper in this place. Pliny observes, that the hind with young is by instinct directed to a certain herb, named seselis, which facilitates the birth. Thunder, also, which looks like the more immediate hand of Providence, has the same effect. <reference osisRef="Psa.29.9">Psa 29:9</reference> : "The Voice of the Lord maketh the Hinds to Calve." See Dr. Young. What is called the wild goat, יעל yael, from עלה alah, to ascend, go or mount up, is generally understood to be the ibex or mountain goat, called yael, from the wonderful manner in which it mounts to the tops of the highest rocks. It is certain, says Johnston, there is no crag of the mountains so high, prominent or steep, but this animal will mount it in a number of leaps, provided only it be rough, and have protuberances large enough to receive its hoofs in leaping. This animal is indigenous to Arabia, is of amazing strength and agility, and considerably larger than the common goat. Its horns are very long, and often bend back over the whole body of the animal; and it is said to throw itself from the tops of rocks or towers, and light upon its horns, without receiving any damage. It goes five months with young. <div eID="gen17927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17928" type="x-p"/> When the hinds do calve? - The hind is the female of the stag, or cervus elaphus, and goes eight months with young. They live to thirty-five or forty years. Incredible longevity has been attributed to some stags. One was taken by Charles VI., in the forest of Senlis, about whose neck was a collar with this inscription, Caesar hoc mihi donavit, which led some to believe that this animal had lived from the days of some one of the twelve Caesars, emperors of Rome. I have seen the following form of this inscription: - <div eID="gen17928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17929" type="x-p"/> Tempore quo Caesar Roma dominatus in alta <div eID="gen17929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17930" type="x-p"/> Aureolo jussit collum signare monili; <div eID="gen17930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17931" type="x-p"/> Nehemiah depascentem quisquis me gramina laedat. <div eID="gen17931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17932" type="x-p"/> Caesaris heu! caussa periturae parcere vitae! <div eID="gen17932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17933" type="x-p"/> Which has been long public in the old English ballad strain, thus: - "When Julius Caesar reigned king, <div eID="gen17933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17934" type="x-p"/> About my neck he put this ring; <div eID="gen17934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17935" type="x-p"/> That whosoever should me take <div eID="gen17935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17936" type="x-p"/> Would save my life for Caesar's sake." <div eID="gen17936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17937" type="x-p"/> Aristotle mentions the longevity of the stag, but thinks it fabulous.
entries.f6cc2eb2523f1b4102ab3d766bff3c5f0a22ac33: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17938" type="x-p"/> They bow themselves - In order to bring forth their young ones. <div eID="gen17938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17939" type="x-p"/> They cast out their sorrows - חבליהם chebleyhem; the placenta, afterbirth, or umbilical cord. So this word has been understood.
entries.5f18462372c0e675d563f0d39b5d826cb0593550: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17940" type="x-p"/> In good liking - After the fawns have sucked for some time, the dam leads them to the pastures, where they feed on different kinds of herbage; but not on corn, for they are not born before harvest-time in Arabia and Palestine, and the stag does not feed on corn, but on grass, moss, and the shoots of the fir, beech, and other trees: therefore the word בר bar, here translated corn, should be translated the open field or country. See Parkhurst. Their nurslings bound away - Mr. Good. In a short time they become independent of the mother, leave her, and return no more. The spirit of the questions in these verses appears to be the following: - Understandest thou the cause of breeding of the mountain goats, etc.? Art thou acquainted with the course and progress of the parturition, and the manner in which the bones grow, and acquire solidity in the womb? See Mr. Good's observations. Houbigant's version appears very correct: (Knowest thou) "how their young ones grow up, increase in the fields, and once departing, return to them no more?"
entries.aa5ed879a12724e90993d292e07483c58f7be2eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17941" type="x-p"/> Who hath sent out the wild ass free? - פרא pere, which we translate wild ass, is the same as the ονος αγριος of the Greeks, and the onager of the Latins; which must not, says Buffon, be confounded with the zebra, for this is an animal of a different species from the ass. The wild ass is not striped like the zebra, nor so elegantly shaped. There are many of those animals in the deserts of Libya and Numidia: they are of a gray color; and run so swiftly that no horse but the Arab barbs can overtake them. Wild asses are found in considerable numbers in East and South Tartary, in Persia, Syria, the islands of the Archipelago, and throughout Mauritania. They differ from tame asses only in their independence and liberty, and in their being stronger and more nimble: but in their shape they are the same. See on <reference osisRef="Job.6.5">Job 6:5</reference> (note). <div eID="gen17941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17942" type="x-p"/> The bands of the wild ass? - ערוד arod, the brayer, the same animal, but called thus because of the frequent and peculiar noise he makes. But Mr. Good supposes this to be a different animal from the wild ass, (the jichta or equus hemionus), which is distinguished by having solid hoofs, a uniform color, no cross on the back, and the tail hairy only at the tip. The ears and tail resemble those of the zebra; the hoofs and body, those of the ass; and the limbs, those of the horse. It inhabits Arabia, China, Siberia, and Tartary, in glassy saline plains or salt wastes, as mentioned in the following verse.
entries.8dc7b8cc1b928bcebdd50a46fd9b5343f57f20de: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17943" type="x-p"/> Whose house - Habitation, or place of resort. <div eID="gen17943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17944" type="x-p"/> The barren land - מלחה melechah, the salt land, or salt places, as in the margin. See above.
entries.221cf83a99e17c5784446ba4e81b7c51a7d5cfc4: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17945" type="x-p"/> He scorneth the multitude - He is so swift that he cannot be run or hunted down. See the description in <reference osisRef="Job.39.5">Job 39:5</reference> (note).
entries.31c9e36aeb34d57549f57a439572d7f69010e1e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17946" type="x-p"/> The range of the mountains - The mountains and desert places are his peculiar places of pasture; and he lives on any thing that is green, or any kind of vegetable production.
entries.11aa12fbc6b8a2a68860bb684f2acac35db570db: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17947" type="x-p"/> Will the unicorn be willing to serve thee? - The "fine elegant animal like a horse, with one long rich curled horn growing out of his forehead," commonly called the unicorn, must be given up as fabulous. The heralds must claim him as their own; place him in their armorial bearings as they please, to indicate the unreal actions, fictitious virtues, and unfought martial exploits of mispraised men. It is not to the honor of the royal arms of Great Britain that this fabulous animal should be one of their supporters. The animal in question, called רים reim, is undoubtedly the rhinoceros, who has the latter name from the horn that grows on his nose. The rhinoceros is known by the name of reim in Arabia to the present day. He is allowed to be a savage animal, showing nothing of the intellect of the elephant. His horn enables him to combat the latter with great success; for, by putting his nose under the elephant's belly, he can rip him up. His skin is like armor, and so very hard as to resist sabres, javelins, lances, and even musket-balls; the only penetrable parts being the belly, the eyes, and about the ears. <div eID="gen17947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17948" type="x-p"/> Or abide by thy crib? - These and several of the following expressions are intended to point out his savage, untameable nature.
entries.eb8b4c18187a09ebefc24fb2e2b71c15ad572f45: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17949" type="x-p"/> Canst thou bind the unicorn - in the furrow? - He will not plough, nor draw in the yoke with another? nor canst thou use him singly, to harrow the ground.
entries.c4daaea2d2e346a0ea16de53d98daa7f84909dcd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17950" type="x-p"/> That he will bring home thy seed - Thou canst make no domestic nor agricultural use of him.
entries.8bd853a25eedaf8e0bdd0d35db95292a0bc78fca: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17951" type="x-p"/> The goodly wings unto the peacocks? - I believe peacocks are not intended here; and the Hebrew word רננים renanim should be translated ostriches; and the term חסידה chasidah, which we translate ostrich, should be, as it is elsewhere translated, stork; and perhaps the word נצה notsah, rendered here feathers, should be translated hawk, or pelican. The Vulgate has, Penna struthionis similis est pennis herodii et accipitris; "the feather of the ostrich is like to that of the stork and the hawk." The Chaldee has, "The wing of the wild cock, who crows and claps his wings, is like to the wing of the stork and the hawk." The Septuagint, not knowing what to make of these different terms, have left them all untranslated, so as to make a sentence without sense. Mr. Good has come nearest both to the original and to the meaning, by translating thus: - "The wing of the ostrich tribe is for flapping; <div eID="gen17951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17952" type="x-p"/> But of the stork and falcon for flight." <div eID="gen17952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17953" type="x-p"/> Though the wings of the ostrich, says he, cannot raise it from the ground, yet by the motion here alluded to, by a perpetual vibration, or flapping - by perpetually catching or drinking in the wind, (as the term נעלסה neelasah implies, which we render goodly), they give it a rapidity of running beyond that possessed by any other animal in the world. Adanson informs us, that when he was at the factory in Padore, he was in possession of two tame ostriches; and to try their strength, says he, "I made a full-grown negro mount the smallest, and two others the largest. This burden did not seem at all disproportioned to their strength. At first they went a pretty high trot; and, when they were heated a little, they expanded their wings, as if it were to catch the wind, and they moved with such fleetness as to seem to be off the ground. And I am satisfied that those ostriches would have distanced the fleetest race-horses that were ever bred in England." <div eID="gen17953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17954" type="x-p"/> As to נצה notsah, here translated falcon, Mr. Good observes, that the term naz is used generally by the Arabian writers to signify both falcon and hawk; and there can be little doubt that such is the real meaning of the Hebrew word; and that it imports various species of the falcon family, as jer-falcon, gos-hawk, and sparrow-hawk. "The argument drawn from natural history advances from quadrupeds to birds; and of birds, those only are selected for description which are most common to the country in which the scene lies, and at the same time are most singular in their properties. Thus the ostrich is admirably contrasted with the stork and the eagle, as affording us an instance of a winged animal totally incapable of flight, but endued with an unrivalled rapidity of running, compared with birds whose flight is proverbially fleet, powerful, and persevering. Let man, in the pride of his wisdom, explain or arraign this difference of construction. "Again, the ostrich is peculiarly opposed to the stork and to some species of the eagle in another sense, and a sense adverted to in the verses immediately ensuing; for the ostrich is well known to take little or no care of its eggs, or of its young, while the stork ever has been, and ever deserves to be, held in proverbial repute for its parental tenderness. The Hebrew word חסידה chasidah, imports kindness or affection; and our own term stork, if derived from the Greek στοργη, storge, as some pretend, has the same original meaning." - Good's Job.
entries.313933a45f1f2a6b615de44567d059f0ee226516: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17955" type="x-p"/> Which leaveth her eggs in the earth - This want of parental affection in the ostrich is almost universally acknowledged. Mr. Jackson, in his Account of Morocco, observes: "The ostrich, having laid her eggs, goes away, forgetting or forsaking them: and if some other ostrich discover them, she hatches them as if they were her own, forgetting probably whether they are or are not; so deficient is the recollection of this bird." This illustrates <reference osisRef="Job.39.15">Job 39:15</reference> : "And forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may break them." The poet seems well acquainted with every part of the subject on which he writes; and facts incontestable confirm all he says. For farther illustration, see the account from Dr. Shaw at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job 39:30</reference> (note).
entries.14afa36eec1b5c2ef5a11303f57f0b0be9679a95: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17956" type="x-p"/> She is hardened against her young - See before, and the extracts from Dr. Shaw at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job 39:30</reference> (note). She neglects her little ones, which are often found half starved, straggling, and moaning about, like so many deserted orphans, for their mother.
entries.602d2455fe528689013f02da83d6f212d32c5c0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17957" type="x-p"/> God hath deprived her of wisdom - Of this foolishness we have an account from the ancients; and here follow two instances: <div eID="gen17957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17958" type="x-p"/> 1. It covers its head in the reeds, and thinks itself all out of sight because itself cannot see. So Claudian: - - 'Stat lumine clauso <div eID="gen17958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17959" type="x-p"/> Ridendum revoluta caput: creditque latere <div eID="gen17959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17960" type="x-p"/> Quad non ipsa videt.' <div eID="gen17960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17961" type="x-p"/> 2. They who hunt them draw the skin of an ostrich's neck on one hand, which proves a sufficient lure to take them with the other. They have so little brain that Heliogabalus had six hundred heads for his supper. Here we may observe, that our judicious as well as sublime author just touches the great points of distinction in each creature, and then hastens to another. A description is exact when you cannot add but what is common to another thing; nor withdraw, but something peculiarly belonging to the thing described. A likeness is lost in too much description, as a meaning is often in too much illustration." - Dr. Young.
entries.2b5949e33e5369c031bbdccb1c3eac6cdd258402: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17962" type="x-p"/> She lifteth up herself - When she raiseth up herself to run away. Proofs of the fleetness of this bird have already been given. It neither flies nor runs distinctly, but has a motion composed of both; and, using its wings as sails, makes great speed. So Claudian: - <div eID="gen17962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17963" type="x-p"/> Vasta velut Libyae venantum vocibus ales <div eID="gen17963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17964" type="x-p"/> Cum premitur, calidas cursu transmittit arenas, <div eID="gen17964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17965" type="x-p"/> Inque modum veli sinuatis flamine pennis <div eID="gen17965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17966" type="x-p"/> Pulverulenta volat. "Xenophon says, Cyrus had horses that could overtake the goat and the wild ass; but none that could reach this creature. A thousand golden ducats, or a hundred camels, was the stated price of a horse that could equal their speed." - Dr. Young.
entries.752fb719ac7bbea1597c2c6336be16256c9d4fcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen17966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17967" type="x-p"/> Hast thou given the horse strength? - Before I proceed to any observations, I shall give Mr. Good's version of this, perhaps inimitable, description: - <reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job 39:19</reference> Hast thou bestowed on the horse mettle?Hast thou clothed his neck with the thunder flash? <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference> Hast thou given him to launch forth as an arrow?Terrible is the pomp of his nostrils. <reference osisRef="Job.39.21">Job 39:21</reference> He paweth in the valley, and exulteth.Boldly he advanceth against the clashing host: <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job 39:22</reference> He mocketh at fear, and trembleth not:Nor turneth he back from the sword. <reference osisRef="Job.39.23">Job 39:23</reference> Against him rattleth the quiver,The glittering spear, and the shield: <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">Job 39:24</reference> With rage and fury he devoureth the ground;And is impatient when the trumpet soundeth. <reference osisRef="Job.39.25">Job 39:25</reference> He exclaimeth among the trumpets, Aha!And scenteth the battle afar off,The thunder of the chieftains, and the shouting. <div eID="gen17967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17968" type="x-p"/> In the year 1713, a letter was sent to the Guardian, which makes No. 86 of that work, containing a critique on this description, compared with similar descriptions of Homer and Virgil. I shall give the substance of it here: - <div eID="gen17968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17969" type="x-p"/> The great Creator, who accommodated himself to those to whom he vouchsafed to speak, hath put into the mouths of his prophets such sublime sentiments and exalted language as must abash the pride and wisdom of man. In the book of Job, the most ancient poem in the world, we have such paintings and descriptions as I have spoken of in great variety. I shall at present make some remarks on the celebrated description of the horse, in that holy book; and compare it with those drawn by Homer and Virgil. <div eID="gen17969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17970" type="x-p"/> Homer hath the following similitude of a horse twice over in the Iliad, which Virgil hath copied from him; at least he hath deviated less from Homer than Mr. Dryden hath from him: - Ὡς δ' ὁτε τις στατος ἱππος, ακοστησας επι φατνη, Δεσμον απορῥηξας θειει πεδιοιο κροαινων, Ειωθως λουεσθαι εΰρῥειος ποταμοιο, Κυδιοων· ὑψου δε καρη εχει, αμοι δε χαιται Ωμοις αΐσσονται· ὁ δ' αγλαΐῃφι πεποιθως Ῥιμφα ἑ γουνα φερει μετα τ' ηθεα και νομον ἱππων. <div eID="gen17970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17971" type="x-p"/> Hom. Il. lib. vi., ver. 506; and lib. xv., ver. 263. <div eID="gen17971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17972" type="x-p"/> Freed from his keepers, thus with broken reins <div eID="gen17972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17973" type="x-p"/> The wanton courser prances o'er the plains, <div eID="gen17973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17974" type="x-p"/> Or in the pride of youth o'erleaps the mound, <div eID="gen17974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17975" type="x-p"/> And snuffs the female in forbidden ground; <div eID="gen17975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17976" type="x-p"/> Or seeks his watering in the well-known flood, <div eID="gen17976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17977" type="x-p"/> To quench his thirst, and cool his fiery blood; <div eID="gen17977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17978" type="x-p"/> He swims luxuriant in the liquid plain, <div eID="gen17978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17979" type="x-p"/> And o'er his shoulders flows his waving mane; <div eID="gen17979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17980" type="x-p"/> He neighs, he snorts, he bears his head on high; <div eID="gen17980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17981" type="x-p"/> Before his ample chest the frothy waters fly. <div eID="gen17981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17982" type="x-p"/> Virgil's description is much fuller than the foregoing, which, as I said, is only a simile; whereas Virgil professes to treat of the nature of the horse: - - Tum, si qua sonum procul arma dedere, <div eID="gen17982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17983" type="x-p"/> Stare loco nescit: micat auribus, et tremit artus <div eID="gen17983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17984" type="x-p"/> Collectumque premens volvit sub naribus ignem: <div eID="gen17984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17985" type="x-p"/> Densa juba, et dextro jactata recumbit in armo. <div eID="gen17985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17986" type="x-p"/> At duplex agitur per lumbos spina, cavatque <div eID="gen17986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17987" type="x-p"/> Tellurem, et solido graviter sonat ungula cornu. <div eID="gen17987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17988" type="x-p"/> Virg. Georg. lib. iii., ver. 83. <div eID="gen17988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17989" type="x-p"/> Which is thus admirably translated: - <div eID="gen17989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17990" type="x-p"/> The fiery courser, when he hears from far <div eID="gen17990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17991" type="x-p"/> The sprightly trumpets, and the shouts of war, <div eID="gen17991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17992" type="x-p"/> Pricks up his ears; and, trembling with delight, <div eID="gen17992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17993" type="x-p"/> Shifts pace, and paws, and hopes the promised fight. <div eID="gen17993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17994" type="x-p"/> On his right shoulder his thick mane reclined, <div eID="gen17994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17995" type="x-p"/> Ruffles at speed, and dances in the wind. <div eID="gen17995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17996" type="x-p"/> His horny hoofs are jetty black and round; <div eID="gen17996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17997" type="x-p"/> His chin is double: starting with a bound, <div eID="gen17997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17998" type="x-p"/> He turns the turf, and shakes the solid ground. <div eID="gen17998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17999" type="x-p"/> Fire from his eyes, clouds from his nostrils flow; <div eID="gen17999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18000" type="x-p"/> He bears his rider headlong on the foe. <div eID="gen18000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18001" type="x-p"/> Now follows that in the Book of Job, which, under all the disadvantages of having been written in a language little understood, of being expressed in phrases peculiar to a part of the world whose manner of thinking and speaking seems to us very uncouth; and, above all, of appearing in a prose translation; is nevertheless so transcendently above the heathen descriptions, that hereby we may perceive how faint and languid the images are which are formed by human authors, when compared with those which are figured, as it were, just as they appear in the eye of the Creator. God, speaking to Job, asks him: - [To do our translators as much justice as possible, and to help the critic, I shall throw it in the hemistich form, in which it appears in the Hebrew, and in which all Hebrew poetry is written.] <reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job 39:19</reference> Hast thou given to the Horse strength?Hast thou clothed his neck with thunder? <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference> Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper?The glory of his nostrils is terrible! <reference osisRef="Job.39.21">Job 39:21</reference> He paweth in the valley, and rejoiceth in strength:He goeth on to meet the armed men. <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job 39:22</reference> He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted:Neither turneth he back from the sword. <reference osisRef="Job.39.23">Job 39:23</reference> Against him rattleth the quiver,The glittering spear and the shield. <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">Job 39:24</reference> He swalloweth the ground with rage and fierceness:Nor doth he believe that it is the sound of the trumpet. <reference osisRef="Job.39.25">Job 39:25</reference> He saith among the trumpets, Heach!And from afar he scenteth the battle,The thunder of the captains, and the shouting. <div eID="gen18001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18002" type="x-p"/> Here are all the great and sprightly images that thought can form of this generous beast, expressed in such force and vigor of style as would have given the great wits of antiquity new laws for the sublime, had they been acquainted with these writings. I cannot but particularly observe that whereas the classical poets chiefly endeavor to paint the outward figure, lineaments, and motions, the sacred poet makes all the beauties to flow from an inward principle in the creature he describes; and thereby gives great spirit and vivacity to his description. The following phrases and circumstances are singularly remarkable: - <reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job 39:19</reference> Hast thou clothed his neck with thunder? <div eID="gen18002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18003" type="x-p"/> Homer and Virgil mention nothing about the neck of the horse but his mane. The sacred author, by the bold figure of thunder, not only expresses the shaking of that remarkable beauty in the horse, and the flakes of hair, which naturally suggest the idea of lightning; but likewise the violent agitation and force of the neck, which in the oriental tongues had been flatly expressed by a metaphor less bold than this. <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference> Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? - There is a twofold beauty in this expression, which not only marks the courage of this beast, by asking if he can be scared; but likewise raises a noble image of his swiftness, by insinuating that, if he could be frightened, he would bound away with the nimbleness of a grasshopper. <div eID="gen18003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18004" type="x-p"/> The glory of his nostrils is terrible - This is more strong and concise than that of Virgil, which yet is the noblest line that was ever written without inspiration: - <div eID="gen18004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18005" type="x-p"/> Collectumque premens volvit sub naribus ignem. <div eID="gen18005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18006" type="x-p"/> And in his nostrils rolls collected fire. <div eID="gen18006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18007" type="x-p"/> Geor. iii., ver. 85. <reference osisRef="Job.39.21">Job 39:21</reference> He rejoiceth in his strength. <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job 39:22</reference> He mocketh at fear. <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">Job 39:24</reference> Neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet. <reference osisRef="Job.39.25">Job 39:25</reference> He saith among the trumpets, Ha! ha! <div eID="gen18007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18008" type="x-p"/> These are signs of courage, as I said before, flowing from an inward principle. There is a peculiar beauty in his not believing it is the sound of the trumpet: that is, he cannot believe it for joy; but when he is sure of it, and is among the trumpets, he saith, Ha! ha! He neighs, he rejoices. His docility is elegantly painted in his being unmoved at the rattling quiver, the glittering spear, and the shield, <reference osisRef="Job.39.23">Job 39:23</reference>, and is well imitated by Oppian, - who undoubtedly read Job, as Virgil did, - in his Poem on Hunting: - Πως μεν γαρ τε μαχαισιν αρηΐος εκλυεν ἱππος Ηχον εγερσιμοθον δολιχων πολεμηΐον αυλων; Η πως αντα δεδορκεν ασκαρδαμυκτοισιν οπωπαις Αιζηοισι λοχον πεπυκασμενον ὁπλιτησι; Και χαλκον σελαγευντα, και αστραπτοντα σιδηρον; Και μαθεν ευτε μενειν χρειω, ποτε δ' αυτις αρουειν. <div eID="gen18008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18009" type="x-p"/> Oppian Cyneget, lib. i., ver. 206. <div eID="gen18009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18010" type="x-p"/> Now firm the managed war-horse keeps his ground, <div eID="gen18010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18011" type="x-p"/> Nor breaks his order though the trumpet sound! <div eID="gen18011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18012" type="x-p"/> With fearless eye the glittering host surveys, <div eID="gen18012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18013" type="x-p"/> And glares directly at the helmet's blaze. <div eID="gen18013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18014" type="x-p"/> The master's word, the laws of war, he knows; <div eID="gen18014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18015" type="x-p"/> And when to stop, and when to charge the foes. <div eID="gen18015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18016" type="x-p"/> He swalloweth the ground, <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">Job 39:24</reference>, is an expression for prodigious swiftness in use among the Arabians, Job's countrymen, to the present day. The Latins have something like it: - <div eID="gen18016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18017" type="x-p"/> Latumque fuga consumere campum. <div eID="gen18017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18018" type="x-p"/> Nemesian. <div eID="gen18018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18019" type="x-p"/> In flight the extended champaign to consume. <div eID="gen18019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18020" type="x-p"/> Carpere prata fuga. <div eID="gen18020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18021" type="x-p"/> Virg. Georg.
