III., Ver. 142. <div eID="gen18021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18022" type="x-p"/> In flight to crop the meads. - Campumque volatu <div eID="gen18022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18023" type="x-p"/> Cum rapuere, pedum vestigia quaeras. <div eID="gen18023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18024" type="x-p"/> When, in their fight, the champaign they have snatch'd, <div eID="gen18024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18025" type="x-p"/> No track is left behind. <div eID="gen18025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18026" type="x-p"/> It is indeed the boldest and noblest of images for swiftness; nor have I met with any thing that comes so near it as Mr. Pope's, in Windsor Forest: - <div eID="gen18026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18027" type="x-p"/> Th' impatient courser pants in every vein,= <div eID="gen18027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18028" type="x-p"/> And pawing, seems to beat the distant plain; <div eID="gen18028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18029" type="x-p"/> Hills, vales, and floods, appear already cross'd; <div eID="gen18029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18030" type="x-p"/> And ere he starts, a thousand steps are lost. <div eID="gen18030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18031" type="x-p"/> He smelleth the battle afar off, and what follows about the shouting, is a circumstance expressed with great spirit by Lucan: - <div eID="gen18031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18032" type="x-p"/> So when the ring with joyful shouts resounds, <div eID="gen18032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18033" type="x-p"/> With rage and pride th' imprison'd courser bounds; <div eID="gen18033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18034" type="x-p"/> He frets, he foams, he rends his idle rein, <div eID="gen18034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18035" type="x-p"/> Springs o'er the fence, and headlong seeks the plain. <div eID="gen18035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18036" type="x-p"/> This judicious and excellent critique has left me little to say on this sublime description of the horse: I shall add some cursory notes only. In <reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job 39:19</reference> we have the singular image, clothed his neck with thunder. How thunder and the horse's neck can be well assimilated to each other, I confess I cannot see. The author of the preceding critique seems to think that the principal part of the allusion belongs to the shaking of this remarkable beauty (the mane) in a horse; and the flakes of hair, which naturally suggest the idea of lightning. I am satisfied that the floating mane is here meant. The original is רעמה ramah, which Bochart and other learned men translate as above. How much the mane of a horse shaking and waving in the wind adds to his beauty and stateliness, every one is sensible; and the Greek and Latin poets, in their description of the horse, take notice of it. Thus Homer: - - Αμφι δε χαιται Ωμοις αΐσσονται. <div eID="gen18036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18037" type="x-p"/> Iliad vi., ver. 509. "His mane dishevell'd o'er his shoulders flies." <div eID="gen18037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18038" type="x-p"/> And Virgil: - <div eID="gen18038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18039" type="x-p"/> Luduntque per colla, per armos. <div eID="gen18039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18040" type="x-p"/> Aen. xi., ver. 497. <div eID="gen18040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18041" type="x-p"/> The verb רעם raam signifies to toss, to agitate; and may very properly be applied to the mane, for reasons obvious to all. Virgil has seized this characteristic in his fine line, Georg. iii. ver. 86: - <div eID="gen18041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18042" type="x-p"/> Densa juba, et dextro jactata recumbit in armo. "His toss'd thick mane on his right shoulder falls." <div eID="gen18042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18043" type="x-p"/> Naturally, the horse is one of the most timid of animals; and this may be at once accounted for from his small quantity of brain. Perhaps there is no animal of his size that has so little. He acquires courage only from discipline; for naturally he starts with terror and affright at any sudden noise. It requires much discipline to bring him to hear the noise of drums and trumpets, and especially to bear a pair of kettle drums placed on each side his neck, and beaten there, with the most alarming variety of sounds. Query, Does the sacred text allude to any thing of this kind? I have been led to form this thought from the following circumstance. In some ancient MSS. of the Shah Nameh, a most eminent heroic poem, by the poet Ferdoosy, the Homer of India, in my own collection, adorned with paintings, representing regal interviews, animals, battles, etc., there appear in some places representations of elephants, horses, and camels, with a pair of drums, something like our kettle drums, hanging on each side of the animal's neck, and beaten, by a person on the saddle, with two plectrums or drumsticks; the neck itself being literally clothed with the drums and the housings on which they are fixed. Who is it then that has framed the disposition of such a timid animal, that by proper discipline it can bear those thundering sounds, which at first would have scared it to the uttermost of distraction? The capacity to receive discipline and instruction is as great a display of the wisdom of God as the formation of the bodies of the largest, smallest, or most complex animals is of his power. I leave this observation without laying any stress upon it. On such difficult subjects conjecture has a lawful range.
entries.97ff26ff67673b2815ea262315883d1cfdc43acc: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen18043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18044" type="x-p"/> He paweth in the valley - יחפרו yachperu, "they dig in the valley," i.e., in his violent galloping, in every pitch of his body, he scoops up sods out of the earth. Virgil has seized this idea also, in his cavat tellurem; "he scoops out the ground." See before.
entries.2fa086ebb06e7641796bd200f6e9b1f97c67c67f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen18044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18045" type="x-p"/> He saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha - The original is peculiarly emphatical: האח Heach! a strong, partly nasal, partly guttural sound, exactly resembling the first note which the horse emits in neighing. The strong, guttural sounds in this hemistich are exceedingly expressive: האח ומרחוק יריח מלחמה Heach! umerachok yariach milchamah; "Heach, for from afar he scenteth the battle." <div eID="gen18045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18046" type="x-p"/> The reader will perceive that Mr. Good has given a very different meaning to <reference osisRef="Job.39.20">Job 39:20</reference> from that in the present text, Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? by translating the Hebrew thus: - "Hast thou given him to launch forth as an arrow?" <div eID="gen18046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18047" type="x-p"/> The word ארבה arbeh, which we translate locust or grasshopper, and which he derives from רבה rabah, the א aleph being merely formative, he says, "may as well mean an arrow as it does in <reference osisRef="Job.16.13">Job 16:13</reference>, רביו rabbaiv, 'His arrows fly around me.'" The verb רעש raash in the word התועישנו hatharishennu, "Canst thou make him afraid?' he contends, "signifies to tremble, quiver, rush, launch, dart forth; and, taken in this sense, it seems to unite the two ideas of rapidity and coruscation." This is the principal alteration which this learned man has made in the text. <div eID="gen18047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18048" type="x-p"/> I shall conclude on this subject by giving Coverdale's translation: Hast thou geven the horse his strength, or lerned him how to bow down his neck with feare; that he letteth himself be dryven forth like a greshopper, where as the stout neyenge that he maketh is fearfull? He breaketh the grounde with the hoffes of his fete chearfully in his strength, and runneth to mete the harnest men. He layeth aside all feare, his stomach is not abated, neither starteth he aback for eny swerde. Though the qyvers rattle upon him, though the speare and shilde glistre: yet russheth he in fearsley, and beateth upon the grounde. He feareth not the noise of the trompettes, but as soone as he heareth the shawmes blowe, Tush (sayeth he) for he smelleth the batell afarre of, the noyse, the captaynes, and the shoutinge. This is wonderfully nervous, and at the same time accurate.
entries.5ab3de30d1399ee69c8c2e2b82601c11a40bcd68: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen18048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18049" type="x-p"/> Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom - The hawk is called נץ nets, from its swiftness in darting down upon its prey; hence its Latin name, nisus, which is almost the same as the Hebrew. It may very probably mean the falcon, observes Dr. Shaw. The flight of a strong falcon is wonderfully swift. A falcon belonging to the Duke of Cleves flew out of Westphalia into Prussia in one day; and in the county of Norfolk, a hawk has made a flight at a woodcock of near thirty miles in an hour. Thuanus says, "A hawk flew from London to Paris in one night." It was owing to its swiftness that the Egyptians in their hieroglyphics made it the emblem of the wind. <div eID="gen18049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18050" type="x-p"/> Stretch her wings toward the south? - Most of the falcon tribe pass their spring and summer in cold climates; and wing their way toward warmer regions on the approach of winter. This is what is here meant by stretching her wings toward the south. Is it through thy teaching that this or any other bird of passage knows the precise time for taking flight, and the direction in which she is to go in order to come to a warmer climate? There is much of the wisdom and providence of God to be seen in the migration of birds of passage. This has been remarked before. There is a beautiful passage in Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer 8:7</reference>, on the same subject: "The stork in the heavens knoweth her appointed times; and the turtle, and the crane, and the swallow, observe the time of their coming: but my people know not the judgment of the Lord."
entries.604b1d51e83b5f5961f72bdd1a77d63946749fa0: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen18050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18051" type="x-p"/> Doth the eagle mount up - The eagle is said to be of so acute a sight, that when she is so high in the air that men cannot see her, she can discern a small fish in the water! See on <reference osisRef="Job.39.29">Job 39:29</reference> (note).
entries.cf6e28dd1a85c364fd52fe289fd57cdd616a948d: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen18051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18052" type="x-p"/> Upon the crag of the rock - שן סלע shen sela, the tooth of the rock, i.e., some projecting part, whither adventurous man himself dares not follow her. <div eID="gen18052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18053" type="x-p"/> And the strong place - ומצודה umetsudah. Mr. Good translates this word ravine, and joins it to <reference osisRef="Job.39.29">Job 39:29</reference>, thus: "And thence espieth the ravine: her eyes trace the prey afar off."
entries.850084ae0d33b8e975048fdffa7288fef85b23c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen18053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18054" type="x-p"/> Her eyes behold afar off - The eagle was proverbial for her strong and clear sight. So Horace, lib. i., sat. iii., ver. 25: - <div eID="gen18054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18055" type="x-p"/> Cum tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, <div eID="gen18055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18056" type="x-p"/> Cur in amicorum vitas tam cernis acutum, <div eID="gen18056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18057" type="x-p"/> Quam aut aquila, aut serpens Epidaurius? "For wherefore while you carelessly pass by <div eID="gen18057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18058" type="x-p"/> Your own worst vices with unheeding eye, <div eID="gen18058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18059" type="x-p"/> Why so sharp-sighted in another's fame, <div eID="gen18059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18060" type="x-p"/> Strong as an eagle's ken, or dragon's beam?" <div eID="gen18060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18061" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen18061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18062" type="x-p"/> So Aelian, lib. i., cap. 42. And Homer, Iliad xvii., calls the eagle οξυτατον ὑπουρανιων πετεηνων, "The most quick-sighted of all fowls under heaven."
entries.cbd9c1708611e51d4f927157873c9e6931741ef7: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen18062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18063" type="x-p"/> Her young ones also suck up blood - The eagle does not feed her young with carrion, but with prey newly slain, so that they may suck up blood. <div eID="gen18063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18064" type="x-p"/> Where the slain are, there is she - These words are quoted by our Lord. "Wheresoever the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together," <reference osisRef="Mat.24.28">Mat 24:28</reference> (note). It is likely, however, that this was a proverbial mode of expression; and our Lord adapts it to the circumstances of the Jewish people, who were about to fall a prey to the Romans. See the notes there. <div eID="gen18064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18065" type="x-p"/> In the preceding notes I have referred to Dr. Shaw's account of the ostrich as the most accurate and authentic yet published. With the following description I am sure every intelligent reader will be pleased. "In commenting therefore upon these texts it may be observed, that when the ostrich is full grown, the neck, particularly of the male, which before was almost naked, is now very beautifully covered with red feathers. The plumage likewise upon the shoulders, the back, and some parts of the wings, from being hitherto of a dark grayish color, becomes now as black as jet, whilst the rest of the feathers retain an exquisite whiteness. They are, as described <reference osisRef="Job.39.13">Job 39:13</reference>, the very feathers and plumage of the stork, i.e., they consist of such black and white feathers as the stork, called from thence hdysx chasidah, is known to have. But the belly, the thighs, and the breast, do not partake of this covering, being usually naked, and when touched are of the same warmth as the flesh of quadrupeds. "Under the joint of the great pinion, and sometimes under the less, there is a strong pointed excrescence like a cock's spur, with which it is said to prick and stimulate itself, and thereby acquire fresh strength and vigor whenever it is pursued. But nature seems rather to have intended that, in order to prevent the suffocating effects of too great a plethora, a loss of blood should be consequent thereupon, especially as the ostrich appears to be of a hot constitution, with lungs always confined, and consequently liable to be preter-naturally inflamed upon these occasions. "When these birds are surprised by coming suddenly upon them whilst they are feeding in some valley, or behind some rocky or sandy eminence in the deserts, they will not stay to be curiously viewed and examined. Neither are the Arabs ever dexterous enough to overtake them, even when they are mounted upon their jinse, or horses, as they are called, of family. They, when they raise themselves up for flight, (<reference osisRef="Job.39.18">Job 39:18</reference>), laugh at the horse and his rider. They afford him an opportunity only of admiring at a distance the extraordinary agility and the stateliness of their motions, the richness of their plumage, and the great propriety there was of ascribing to them (<reference osisRef="Job.30.13">Job 30:13</reference>) an expanded quivering wing. Nothing, certainly, can be more beautiful and entertaining than such a sight! The wings, by their repeated though unwearied vibrations, equally serving them for sails and oars; whilst their feet, no less assisting in conveying them out of sight, are in no degree sensible of fatigue. "By the repeated accounts which I often had from my conductors, as well as from Arabs of different places, I have been informed that the ostrich lays from thirty to fifty eggs. Aelian mentions more than eighty, but I never heard of so large a number. The first egg is deposited in the center; the rest are placed as conveniently as possible round about it. In this manner it is said to lay-deposit or thrust (<reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference>) - her eggs in The Earth, and to warm them in the sand, and forgetteth, as they are not placed, like those of some other birds, upon trees or in the clefts of rocks, etc., that the foot of the traveler may crush them, or that the wild beasts may break them. "Yet notwithstanding the ample provision which is hereby made for a numerous offspring, scarce one quarter of these eggs are ever supposed to be hatched; and of those that are, no small share of the young ones may perish with hunger, from being left too early by their dams to shift for themselves. For in these the most barren and desolate recesses of the Sahara, where the ostrich chooses to make her nest, it would not be enough to lay eggs and hatch them, unless some proper food was near at hand, and already prepared for their nourishment. And accordingly we are not to consider this large collection of eggs as if they were all intended for a brood; they are, the greatest part of them, reserved for food, which the dam breaks and disposes of according to the number and the cravings of her young ones. "But yet, for all this, a very little share of that στοργη, or natural affection, which so strongly exerts itself in most other creatures, is observable in the ostrich. For, upon the least distant noise or trivial occasion, she forsakes her eggs, or her young ones, to which perhaps she never returns, or if she do, it may be too late either to restore life to the one, or to preserve the lives of the other. Agreeably to this account, the Arabs meet sometimes with whole nests of these eggs undisturbed; some of which are sweet and good, others are addle and corrupted, others again have their young ones of different growths, according to the time it may be presumed they have been forsaken by the dam. They oftener meet a few of the little ones, no bigger than well-grown pullets, half starved, straggling, and moaning about, like so many distressed orphans, for their mother. And in this manner the ostrich may be said (<reference osisRef="Job.39.16">Job 39:16</reference>) to be hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers; her labor in hatching and attending them so far being vain without fear, or the least concern of what becomes of them afterwards. This want of affection is also recorded, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3">Lam 4:3</reference> : The daughter of my people, says the prophet, is cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. "Neither is this the only reproach that may be due to the ostrich; she is likewise inconsiderate and foolish in her private capacity; particularly in the choice of food, which is frequently highly detrimental and pernicious to her; for she swallows every thing greedily and indiscriminately, whether it be pieces of rags, leather, wood, stone, or iron. When I was at Oram, I saw one off these birds swallow, without any seeming uneasiness or inconvenience, several leaden bullets, as they were thrown upon the floor, scorching hot from the mould, the inner coats of the aesophapus and stomach being probably better stocked with glands and juices than in other animals with shorter necks. They are particularly fond of their own excrement, which they greedily eat up as soon as it is voided. No less fond are they of the dung of hens and other poultry. It seems as if their optic as well as olfactory nerves were less adequate and conducive to their safety and preservation than in other creatures. The Divine providence in this, no less than in other respects, (<reference osisRef="Job.39.17">Job 39:17</reference>), having deprived them of wisdom, neither hath it imparted to them understanding. "Those parts of the Sahara which these birds chiefly frequent are destitute of all manner of food and herbage, except it be some few tufts of coarse grass, or else a few other solitary plants of the laureola, apocynum, and some other kinds; each of which is equally destitute of nourishment; and, in the psalmist's phrase, (<reference osisRef="Psa.129.6">Psa 129:6</reference>), even withereth afore it groweth up. Yet these herbs, notwithstanding their dryness, and want of moisture in their temperature, will sometimes have both their leaves and their stalks studded all over with a great variety of land snails, which may afford them some little refreshment. It is very probable, likewise, that they may sometimes seize upon lizards, serpents, together with insects and reptiles of various kinds. Yet still, considering the great voracity and size of this camel-bird, it is wonderful, not only how the little ones, after they are weaned from the provisions I have mentioned, should be brought up and nourished, but even how those of fuller growth and much better qualified to look out for themselves, are able to subsist. "Their organs of digestion, and particularly the gizzards, which, by their strong friction, will wear away iron itself, show them indeed to be granivorous; but yet they have scarce ever an opportunity to exercise them in this way, unless when they chance to stray, which is very seldom, towards those parts of the country which are sown and cultivated, For these, as they are much frequented by the Arabs at the several seasons of grazing, ploughing, and gathering in the harvest; so they are little visited by as indeed they would be an improper abode for this shy, timorous bird; φιλερημος, a lover of the deserts. This last circumstance in the behavior of the ostrich is frequently alluded to in the Holy Scriptures; particularly <reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Isa 13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">Isa 34:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.20">Isa 43:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">Jer 50:39</reference>; where the word, יענה yaanah, instead of being rendered the ostrich, as it is rightly put in the margin, is called the owl; a word used likewise instead of yaanah or the ostrich, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.16">Lev 11:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deu.14.15">Deu 14:15</reference>. "Whilst I was abroad, I had several opportunities of amusing myself with the actions and behavior of the ostrich. It was very diverting to observe with what dexterity and equipoise of body it would play and frisk about on all occasions. In the heat of the day, particularly it would strut along the sunny side of the house with great majesty. It would be perpetually fanning and priding itself with its quivering expanded wings; and seem at every turn to admire and be in love with its shadow. Even at other times whether walking about or resting itself upon the ground, the wings would continue these fanning vibrating motions, as if they were designed to mitigate and assuage that extraordinary heat wherewith their bodies seem to be naturally affected. "Notwithstanding these birds appear tame and tractable to such persons of the family as were more known and familiar to them, yet they were often very rude and fierce to strangers, especially the poorer sort, whom they would not only endeavor to push down by running furiously upon them; but would not cease to peck at them violently with their bills, and to strike them with their feet; whereby they were frequently very mischievous. For the inward claw, or hoof rather as we may call it, of this avis bisulca, being exceedingly strong pointed and angular, I once saw an unfortunate person who had his belly ripped open by one of these strokes. Whilst they are engaged in these combats and assaults, they sometimes make a fierce, angry, and hissing noise with their throats inflated, and their mouths open; at other times, when less resistance is made they have a chuckling or cackling voice, as in the poultry kind; and thereby seem to rejoice and laugh as it were at the timorousness of their adversary. But during the lonesome part of the night, as if their organs of voice had then attained a quite different tone, they often made a very doleful and hideous noise; which would be sometimes like the roaring of a lion; at other times it would bear a near resemblance to the hoarser voices of other quadrupeds, particularly of the bull and the ox. I have often heard them groan, as if they were in the greatest agonies; an action beautifully alluded to by the Prophet Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.1.8">Mic 1:8</reference>, where it is said, I will make a mourning like the yaanah or ostrich. Yaanah, therefore, and רננים renanim, the names by which the ostrich is known in the Holy Scriptures, may very properly be deduced from ענה anah, and רנן ranan, words which the lexicographi explain by exclamare or clamare fortiter; for the noise made by the ostrich being loud and sonorous, exclamare or clamare fortiter may, with propriety enough, be attributed to it, especially as those words do not seem to denote any certain or determined mode of voice or sound peculiar to any one particular species of animals, but such as may be applicable to them all, to birds as well as to quadrupeds and other creatures." <div eID="gen18065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18066" type="x-p"/> Shaw's Travels, p. 541, edit. 4th. 1757. <div eID="gen18066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18067" type="x-p"/> The subjects in this chapter have been so various and important, that I have been obliged to extend the notes and observations to an unusual length; and yet much is left unnoticed which I wished to have inserted. I have made the best selection I could, and must request those readers who wish for more information to consult zoological writers.  <chapter eID="Job.39"/> <div eID="gen18067" type="x-p"/>

entries.af7f8bca21b56f7e9952c8fb74d75c2da2642d88: <reference osisRef="Job.39.1-Job.4.1">Job 39:1-4   1</reference>  Dost thou know the bearing time of the wild goats of the rock? <div eID="gen8657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8658" type="x-p"/> Observest thou the circles of the hinds?   2  Dost thou number the months which they fulfil, <div eID="gen8658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8659" type="x-p"/> And knowest thou the time of their bringing forth?   3  They bow down, they let their young break through, <div eID="gen8659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8660" type="x-p"/> They cast off their pains.   4  Their young ones gain strength, grow up in the desert, <div eID="gen8660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8661" type="x-p"/> They run away and do not return. <div eID="gen8661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8662" type="x-p"/> The strophe treats of the female chamois or steinbocks, <hi type="italic">ibices</hi> (perhaps including the certainly different kinds of chamois), and stags. The former are called יעלים, from יעל, Arab. <hi type="italic">w‛l</hi> (a secondary formation from עלה, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛lâ</hi>), to mount, therefore: rock-climbers. חולל is <hi type="italic">inf. Pil.:</hi> τὸ ὠδίνειν, comp. the <hi type="italic">Pul</hi>. Job 15:7. שׁמר, to observe, exactly as <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Ecc 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.12">1Sa 1:12</reference>; Zec 11:11. In <reference osisRef="Job.39.2">Job 39:2</reference> the question as to the expiration of the time of bearing is connected with that as to the time of bringing forth. תּספּור, <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.14.16">Job 14:16</reference>; לדתּנה (<hi type="italic">littâna</hi>, like עת = עדתּ) with an euphonic termination for לדתּן, as <reference osisRef="Gen.42.36">Gen 42:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.21.29">Gen 21:29</reference>, and also out of pause, Rth 1:19, Ges. §91, 1, rem. 2. Instead of תּפלּחנה Olsh. wishes to read תּפלּטנה, but this (synon. תמלטנה) would be: they let slip away; the former (synon. תבקענה): they cause to divide, i.e., to break through (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">felâh</hi>, the act of breaking through, freedom, prosperity). On כּרע, to kneel down as the posture of one in travail, vid., 1Sa 4:19. “They cast off their pains” is not meant of an easy working off of the after-pains (Hirz., Schlottm.), but חבל signifies in this phrase, as Schultens has first shown, meton. directly the foetus, as Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥabal</hi>, plur. <hi type="italic">ahbâl</hi>, and ὠδίν, even of a child already grown up, as being the fruit of earlier travail, e.g., in Aeschylus, <hi type="italic">Agam</hi>. 1417f.; even the like phrase, ῥίψαι ὠδῖνα = <hi type="italic">edere foetum,</hi> is found in Euripides, <hi type="italic">Ion</hi> 45. Thus born with ease, the young animals grow rapidly to maturity (חלם, <hi type="italic">pinguescere, pubescere,</hi> whence חלום, a dream as the result of puberty, vid., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 282), grow in the desert (בּבּר, Targ. = בּחוּץ, vid., i. 329, note), seek the plain, and return not again למו, <hi type="italic">sibi h. e. sui juris esse volentes</hi> (Schult.), although it might also signify <hi type="italic">ad eas</hi>, for the Hebr. is rather confused on the question of the distinction of gender, and even in חבליהם and בניהם the <hi type="italic">masc</hi>. is used ἐπικοίνως. We, however, prefer to interpret according to <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>; Job 24:16. Moreover, Bochart is right: <hi type="italic">Non hic agitur de otiosa et mere speculativa cognitione, sed de ea cognitione, quae Deo propria est, qua res omnes non solum novit, sed et dirigit atque gubernat.  </hi>
entries.871a5d21f64fbb6fddb4efb48628b297fb0dba24: <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.8.5">Job 39:5-8   5</reference>  Who hath sent forth the wild ass free, <div eID="gen8662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8663" type="x-p"/> And who loosed the bands of the wild ass,   6  Whose house I made the steppe, <div eID="gen8663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8664" type="x-p"/> And his dwelling the salt country?   7  He scorneth the tumult of the city, <div eID="gen8664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8665" type="x-p"/> He heareth not the noise of the driver.   8  That which is seen upon the mountains is his pasture, <div eID="gen8665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> And he sniffeth after every green thing. <div eID="gen8666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8667" type="x-p"/> On the wild ass (not: ass of the forest).<note placement="foot">It is a dirty yellow with a white belly, single-hoofed and long-eared; its hornless head somewhat resembles that of the gazelle, but is much later; its hair has the dryness of the hair of the deer, and the animal forms the transition from the stag and deer genus to the ass. It is entirely distinct from the mahâ or baqar el-wahsh, wild ox, whose large soft eyes are so much celebrated by the poets of the steppe. This latter is horned and double-hoofed, and forms the transition from the stag to the ox distinct from the <hi type="italic">ri'm</hi>, ראם, therefore perhaps an antelope of the kind of the Indian <hi type="italic">nîlgau</hi>, blue ox, <hi type="italic">Portax tragocamelus</hi>. I have not seen both kinds of animals alive, but I have often seen their skins in the tents of the <hi type="italic">Ruwalâ</hi>. Both kinds are remarkable for their very swift running, and it is especially affirmed of the <hi type="italic">ferâ</hi> that no rider can overtake it. The poets compare a troop of horsemen that come rushing up and vanish in the next moment to a herd of <hi type="italic">ferâ</hi>. In spite of its difficulty and hazardousness, the nomads are passionately given to hunting the wild ass, and the proverb cited by the Kâmûs: <hi type="italic">kull es - sêd bigôf el - ferâ</hi> (every hunt sticks in the belly of the <hi type="italic">ferâ</hi>, i.e., compared with that, every other hunt is nothing), is perfectly correct. When the approach of a herd, which always consists of several hundred, is betrayed by a cloud of dust which can be seen many miles off, so many horsemen rise up from all sides in pursuit that the animals are usually scattered, and single ones are obtained by the dogs and by shots. The herd is called <hi type="italic">gemı̂le</hi>, and its leader is called <hi type="italic">‛anûd</hi> (ענוּד),as with gazelles. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8668" type="x-p"/> In Hebr. and Arab. it is פּרא (<hi type="italic">ferâ</hi> or <hi type="italic">himâr el - wahsh ,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">asinus ferus</hi>), and Aram. ערוד; the former describes it as a swift-footed animal, the latter as an animal shy and difficult to be tamed by the hand of man; “Kulan” is its Eastern Asiatic name. lxx correctly translates: τίς δὲ ἐστιν ὁ ἀφεὶς ὄνον ἄγριον ἐλεύθερον. חפשׁי is the <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of the predicate (comp. <reference osisRef="Gen.33.2">Gen 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.30">Jer 22:30</reference>). Parallel with ערבה (according to its etymon perhaps, land of darkness, <hi type="italic">terra incognita</hi>) is מלחה, salt <hi type="italic">adj</hi>. or (sc. ארץ) a salt land, i.e., therefore unfruitful and incapable of culture, as the country round the Salt Sea of Palestine: that the wild ass even gladly licks the salt or natron of the desert, is a matter of fact, and may be assumed, since all wild animals that feed on plants have a partiality, which is based on chemical laws of life, for licking slat. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.8">Job 39:8</reference></hi> Ew. observes, to render יתוּר as “what is espied” is insecure, “on account of the structure of the verse” (<hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. S. 419, Anm.). This reason is unintelligible; and in general there is no reason for rendering יתוּר, after lxx, Targ., Jer., and others, as an Aramaic 3 <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. with a mere half vowel instead of Kametz before the tone = יתוּר, which is without example in Old Testament Hebrew (for יהוּא, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.3">Ecc 11:3</reference>, follows the analogy of יהי), but יתוּר signifies either <hi type="italic">abundantia</hi> (after the form יבוּל, לחוּם <reference osisRef="Job.20.23">Job 20:23</reference>, from יתר, Arab. <hi type="italic">wtr</hi>, p. 571) or <hi type="italic">investigabile</hi>, what can be searched out (after the form יקוּם, that which exists, from תּוּר, Arab. <hi type="italic">târ</hi>, to go about, look about), which, with Olsh. §212, and most expositors, we prefer.
entries.68c7b5293ae331080206f65db7a4ef644e881b9b: <reference osisRef="Job.39.9-Job.12.9">Job 39:9-12   9</reference>  Will the oryx be willing to serve thee, <div eID="gen8668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8669" type="x-p"/> Or will he lodge in thy crib? 10  Canst thou bind the oryx in the furrow with a leading rein, <div eID="gen8669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8670" type="x-p"/> Or will he harrow the valleys, following thee? 11  Wilt thou trust him because his strength is great, <div eID="gen8670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8671" type="x-p"/> And leave thy labour to him? 12  Wilt thou confide in him to bring in thy sowing, <div eID="gen8671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8672" type="x-p"/> And to garner thy threshing-floor? <div eID="gen8672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8673" type="x-p"/> In correct texts רים has a <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Resh</hi>, and היאבה the accent on the <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.21">Pro 11:21</reference> ינּקה רע, and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.12">Jer 39:12</reference> רּע מאוּמה. The tone retreats according to the rule, Ges. §29, 3, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; and the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> is, as also when the second word begins with an aspirate,<note placement="foot">The National Grammarians call this exception to the rule, that the <hi type="italic">muta</hi> is aspirated when the preceding word ends with a vowel, אתי מרחיק (<hi type="italic">veniens e longinquo</hi>), i.e., the case, where the word ending with a vowel is <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, whether from the very first, or, when the second word is a monosyllable or has the tone on the <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> on account of the accent that has retreated (in order to avoid two syllables with the chief tone coming together); in this case the aspirate, and in general the initial letter (if capable of being doubled) of the second monosyllabic or <hi type="italic">penultima</hi>-accented word, takes a <hi type="italic">Dagesh;</hi> but this is not without exceptions that are quite as regular. Regularly, the second word is not dageshed if it begins with ו, כ, ל, ב, or if the first word is only a bare verb, e.g., עשׂה לו, or one that has only ו before it, e.g., ועשׂה פסח; the tone of the first word in both these examples retreats, but without the initial of the second being doubled. This is supplementary, and as far as necessary a correction, to what is said in <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, i 392, Anm.</note><hi type="italic">Dag. forte conj.,</hi> which the <hi type="italic">Resh</hi> also takes, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.1">Pro 15:1</reference> מענה־רּך, exceptionally, according to the rule, Ges. §20, 2, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. In all, it occurs thirteen times with <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> in the Old Testament - a relic of a mode of pointing which treated the ר (as in Arabic) as a letter capable of being doubled (Ges. §22, 5), that has been supplanted in the system of pointing that gained the ascendency. רים (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.22">Psa 22:22</reference>, רם) is contracted from ראם (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.11">Psa 92:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, ראים), which (= ראם) is of like form with Arab. <hi type="italic">ri'm</hi> (Olsh. §154, <hi type="italic">a</hi>).<note placement="foot">Since <hi type="italic">ra'ima</hi>, inf. <hi type="italic">ri'mân</hi>, has the signification <hi type="italic">assuescere</hi>, ראם, רים, רימנא (Targ.) might describe the oryx as a gregarious animal, although all ruminants have this characteristic in common. On ראם, Arab. <hi type="italic">r'm ,</hi> vid., Seetzen’s Reise, iii. S. 393, Z 9ff., and also iv. 496.</note> <div eID="gen8673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8674" type="x-p"/> Such, in the present day in Syria, is the name of the gazelle that is for the most part white with a yellow back and yellow stripes in the face (<hi type="italic">Antilope leucoryx</hi>, in distinction from Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ifrı̂</hi>, the earth-coloured, dirty-yellow <hi type="italic">Antilope oryx</hi>, and Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥmrı̂ , himrı̂ ,</hi> the deer-coloured <hi type="italic">Antilope dorcas</hi>); the Talmud also (<hi type="italic">b. Zebachim</hi>, 113b; <hi type="italic">Bathra</hi>, 74 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) combines ראימא and אורזילא or ארזילא, a gazelle (Arab. <hi type="italic">gazâl</hi>), and therefore reckons the <hi type="italic">reêm</hi> to the antelope genus, of which the gazelle is a species; and the question, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.10">Job 39:10</reference></hi>, shows that an animal whose home is on the mountains is intended, viz., as Bochart, and recently Schlottm. (making use of an academic treatise of Lichtenstein on the antelopes, 1824), has proved, the oryx, which the lxx also probably understands when it translates μονοκέρως; for the Talmud. קרש, mutilated from it, is, according to <hi type="italic">Chullin</hi>, 59 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, a one-horned animal, and is more closely defined as טביא דבי עילאי, “gazelle (antelope) of Be (Beth)-Illâi” (comp. Lewysohn, <hi type="italic">Zoologie des Talmuds</hi>, 1858, §146). <div eID="gen8674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8675" type="x-p"/> The oryx also appears on Egyptian monuments sometimes with two horns, but mostly with one variously curled; and both Aristotle<note placement="foot">Vid., Sundevall, <hi type="italic">Die Thierarten des Aristoteles</hi> (Stockholm, 1863), S. 64f.</note> and Pliny describe it as a one-horned cloven-hoof; so that one must assent to the supposition of a one-horned variety of the oryx (although as a fact of natural history it is not yet fully established), as then there is really tolerably certain information of a one-horned antelope both in Upper Asia and in Central Africa;<note placement="foot">J. W. von Müller (<hi type="italic">Das Einhorn von gesch. u. naturwiss. Standpunkte betrachtet,</hi> 1852) believed that in a horn in the Ambras Collection at Vienna he recognised a horn of the Monocerôs (comp. Fechner’s <hi type="italic">Centralblatt,</hi> 1854, Nr. 2), but he is hardly right. J. W. von Müller, Francis Galton (<hi type="italic">Narrative of an Explorer in Tropical South Africa,</hi> 1853), and other travellers have heard the natives speak ingenuously of the unicorn, but without seeing it themselves. On the other hand, Huc and Gabet (<hi type="italic">Journeyings through Mongolia and Thibet</hi>, Germ. edition) tell us “a horn of this animal was sent to Calcutta: it was 50 centimetres long and 11 in circumference; from the root it ran up to a gradually diminishing point. It was almost straight, black, etc ... . Hodgson, when English consul at Nepal, had the good fortune to obtain an unicorn ... . It is a kind of antelope, which in southern Thibet, that borders on Nepal, is called <hi type="italic">Tschiru</hi>. Hodgson sent a skin and horn to Calcutta; they came from an unicorn that died in the menagerie of the Raja of Nepal.” The detailed description follows, and the suggestion is advanced that this <hi type="italic">Antilope Hodgsonii</hi>, as it has been proposed to call the <hi type="italic">Tschiru</hi>, is the one-horned oryx of the ancients. The existence of one-horned wild sheep (not antelopes), attested by R. von Schlagintweit (<hi type="italic">Zoologischer Garten</hi>, 1st year, S. 72), the horn of which consists of two parts gradually growing together, covered by one horn-sheath, does not depreciate the credibility of the account given by Huc-Gabet (to which Prof. Will has called my attention as being the most weighty testimony of the time). Another less minute account is to be found in the Arabic description of a journey (communicated to me by Prof. Fleischer) by Selîm Bisteris (Beirût, 1856): In the menagerie of the Viceroy of Egypt he saw an animal of the colour of a gazelle, but the size and form of an ass, with a long straight horn between the ears, and what, as he says, seldom go together) with hoofs, viz. - and as the expression Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥâfr</hi>, horse’s hoof (not Arab. <hi type="italic">chuff</hi>, a camel’s hoof), also implies - proper, uncloven hoofs, - therefore an one-horned and at the same time one-hoofed antelope.</note> and therefore there is sufficient ground for seeking the origin of the tradition of the unicorn in an antelope, - perhaps rather like a horse, - with one horn rising out of the two points of ossification over the frontal suture. The proper buffalo, <hi type="italic">Bos bubalus,</hi> cannot therefore be intended, because it only came from India to Western Asia and Europe at a more recent date, but also not any other species whatever of this animal (Carey and others), which is recognisable by its flat horns, which are also near together, and its forbidding, staring, bloodshot eyes; for it is tameable, and is (even in modern Syria) used as a domestic animal. On the other hand there are antelopes which somewhat resemble the horse, others the ox (whence βούβαλος, βούβαλις, is a name for the antelope), others the deer and the ass. Schultens erroneously considers ראם to be the buffalo, being misled by a passage in the Divan of the Hudheilites, which gives the <hi type="italic">ri'm</hi> the by-name of <hi type="italic">dhu chadam</hi>, i.e., oxen-like white-footed, which exactly applies to the <hi type="italic">A. oryx</hi> or even the <hi type="italic">A. leucoryx;</hi> for the former has white feet and legs striped lengthwise with black stripes, the latter white feet and legs. Just as little reason is there for imagining the rhinoceros after Aquila (and in part Jerome); ῥινοκέρως is nothing but an unhappy rendering of the μονοκέρως of the lxx. The question in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.10">Job 39:10</reference></hi>, as already observed, requires an animal that inhabits the mountains. <div eID="gen8675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8676" type="x-p"/> On אבה, to be willing = to take up, receive. The “furrow (תּלם, <hi type="italic">sulcus</hi>, not <hi type="italic">porca</hi>, the ridge between the furrows) of his cord” is that which it is said to break up by means of the ploughshare, being led by a rein. אחריך refers to the leader, who goes just before or at the side; according to Hahn, to one who has finished the sowing which precedes the harrowing; but it is more natural to imagine the leader of the animal that is harrowing, which is certainly not left to itself. On כּי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.12">Job 39:12</reference></hi>, as an exponent of the obj. vid., Ew. §336, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> here uses the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> שׁוּב transitively: to bring back (viz., that which was sown as harvested), which is possible (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job 42:10</reference>). גרנך, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.12">Job 39:12</reference></hi>, is either a locative (into thy threshing-floor) or <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of the obj. <hi type="italic">per synecd. continentis pro contento,</hi> as Rth 3:2; Mat 3:12. The position of the question from beginning to end assumes an animal outwardly resembling the yoke-ox, as the ראם is also elsewhere put with the ox, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">Deu 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.29.6">Psa 29:6</reference>; Isa 34:7. But the conclusion at length arrived at by Hahn and in Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>, that on this very account the buffalo is to be understood, is a mistake: <hi type="italic">A. oryx</hi> and <hi type="italic">leucoryx</hi> are both (for this very reason not distinguished by the ancients) entirely similar to the ox; they are not only ruminants, like the ox, with a like form of the hoof, but also of a plump form, which makes them appear to be of the ox tribe.
entries.4142a62c11d24119765dbc0b266d7b6586d29a43: <reference osisRef="Job.39.13-Job.18.13">Job 39:13-18 13</reference>  The wing of the ostrich vibrates joyously, <div eID="gen8676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8677" type="x-p"/> Is she pious, wing and feather? 14  No, she leaveth her eggs in the earth <div eID="gen8677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8678" type="x-p"/> And broodeth over the dust, 15  Forgetting that a foot may crush them, <div eID="gen8678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8679" type="x-p"/> And the beast of the field trample them. 16  She treateth her young ones harshly as if they were not hers; <div eID="gen8679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8680" type="x-p"/> In vain is her labour, without her being distressed. 17  For Eloah hath caused her to forget wisdom, <div eID="gen8680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8681" type="x-p"/> And gave her no share of understanding. 18  At the time when she lasheth herself aloft, <div eID="gen8681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8682" type="x-p"/> She derideth the horse and horseman. <div eID="gen8682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8683" type="x-p"/> As the wild ass and the ox-like oryx cannot be tamed by man, and employed in his service like the domestic ass and ox, so the ostrich, although resembling the stork in its stilt-like structure, the colour of its feathers, and its gregarious life, still has characteristics totally different from those one ought to look for according to this similarity. רננים, a wail, prop. a tremulous shrill sound (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.39.23">Job 39:23</reference>), is a name of the female ostrich, whose peculiar cry is called in Arabic <hi type="italic">zimâr</hi> (זמר). נעלס (from עלס, which in comparison with עלץ, עלז, rarely occurs) signifies to make gestures of joy. אם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.13">Job 39:13</reference></hi>, is an interrogative <hi type="italic">an;</hi> חסידה, <hi type="italic">pia</hi>, is a play upon the name of the stork, which is so called: <hi type="italic">pia instar ciconiae</hi> (on this figure of speech, comp. Mehren’s <hi type="italic">Rehtorik der Araber,</hi> S. 178). כּי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference></hi>, establishes the negation implied in the question, as e.g., Isa 28:28. The idea is not that the hen-ostrich abandons the hatching of her eggs to the earth (עזב ל as <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference>), and makes them “glow over the dust” (Schlottm.), for the maturing energy compensating for the sitting of the parent bird proceeds from the sun’s heat, which ought to have been mentioned; one would also expect a <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. instead of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> תּחמּם, which can be understood only of hatching by her own warmth. The hen-ostrich also really broods herself, although from time to time she abandons the חמּם to the sun.<note placement="foot">It does, however, as it appears, actually occur, that the female leaves the work of hatching to the sun by day, and to the male at night, and does not sit at all herself; vid., Funke’s <hi type="italic">Naturgeschichte</hi>, revised by Taschenberg (1864), S. 243f.</note> <div eID="gen8683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8684" type="x-p"/> That which contrasts with the φιλοστοργία of the stork, which is here made prominent, is that she lays here eggs in a hole in the ground, and partly, when the nest is full, above round about it, while חסידה ברושׁים ביתה, Psa 104:17. רננים is construed in accordance with its meaning as <hi type="italic">fem. sing.,</hi> Ew. §318, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. Since she acts thus, what next happens consistently therewith is told by the not aoristic but only consecutive ותּשׁכּח: and so she forgets that the foot may crush (זוּר, to press together, break by pressure, as הזּוּרה, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.5">Isa 59:5</reference> = הזּוּרה, that which is crushed, comp. לנה = לנה, Zec 5:4) them (i.e., the eggs, Ges. §146, 3), and the beast of the field may trample them down, crush them (דּוּשׁ as Arab. <hi type="italic">dâs</hi>, to crush by treading upon anything, to tread out).
entries.d6533e4f95a4d1aeeedcf7cffb8bf2ffb28d3d15: Job 39:19-25 19  Dost thou give to the horse strength? <div eID="gen8685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8688" type="x-p"/> Dost thou clothe his neck with flowing hair? 20  Dost thou cause him to leap about like the grasshopper? <div eID="gen8688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> The noise of his snorting is a terror! 21  He paweth the ground in the plain, and boundeth about with strength. <div eID="gen8689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8690" type="x-p"/> He advanceth to meet an armed host. 22  He laugheth at fear, and is not affrighted, <div eID="gen8690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> And turneth not back from the sword. 23  The quiver rattleth over him, <div eID="gen8691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> The glittering lance and spear. 24  With fierceness and rage he swalloweth the ground, <div eID="gen8692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> And standeth not still, when the trumpet soundeth. 25  He saith at every blast of the trumpet: Ha, ha! <div eID="gen8693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8694" type="x-p"/> And from afar he scenteth the battle, <div eID="gen8694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8695" type="x-p"/> The thundering of the captains and the shout of war. <div eID="gen8695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8696" type="x-p"/> After the ostrich, which, as the Arabs say, is composed of the nature of a bird and a camel, comes the horse in its heroic beauty, and impetuous lust for the battle, which is likewise an evidence of the wisdom of the Ruler of the world - a wisdom which demands the admiration of men. This passage of the book of Job, says K. Löffler, in his <hi type="italic">Gesch. des Pferdes </hi>(1863), is the oldest and most beautiful description of the horse. It may be compared to the praise of the horse in Hammer-Purgstall’s <hi type="italic">Duftkörner;</hi> it deserves more than this latter the praise of majestic simplicity, which is the first feature of classic superiority. Jer. falsely renders <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job 39:19</reference></hi>: <hi type="italic">aut circumdabis collo ejus hinnitum;</hi> as Schlottm., who also wishes to be so understood: Dost thou adorn his neck with the voice of thunder? The neck (צוּאר, prop. the twister, as Persic <hi type="italic">gerdân , gerdan ,</hi> from צוּר, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣâr</hi>, to twist by pressure, to turn, bend, as Pers. from <hi type="italic">gerdı̂den</hi>, to turn one’s self, twist) has nothing to do with the voice of neighing. But רעמה also does not signify dignity (Ew. 113, <hi type="italic">d</hi>), but the mane, and is not from רעם = ראם = רם, the hair of the mane, as being above, like λοφιά, but from רעם, <hi type="italic">tremere</hi>, the mane as quivering, trembling (Eliz. Smith: the shaking mane); like φόβη, according to Kuhn, cogn. with σόβη, the tail, from φοβεῖν (σοβεῖν), to wag, shake, scare, comp. άΐ́σσεσθαι of the mane, <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. vi. 510.
entries.19f0fdbe61d128450c0e77731d71b1d6c1a0949b: <reference osisRef="Job.39.26-Job.30.26">Job 39:26-30 26</reference>  Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, <div eID="gen8698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> Doth it spread its wings towards the south? 27  Or is it at thy command that the eagle soareth aloft, <div eID="gen8699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8700" type="x-p"/> And buildeth its nest on high? 28  It inhabiteth the rock, and buildeth its nest <div eID="gen8700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> Upon the crag of the rock and fastness. 29  From thence it seeketh food, <div eID="gen8701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> Its eyes see afar off. 30  And its young ones suck up blood; <div eID="gen8702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> And where the slain are, there is it. <div eID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> The ancient versions are unanimous in testifying that, according to the signification of the root, נץ signifies the hawk (which is significant in the Hieroglyphics): the soaring one, the high-flyer (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">nṣṣ</hi>, to rise, struggle forwards, and Arab. <hi type="italic">nḍḍ</hi>, to raise the wings for flight). The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. יאבר- (jussive form in the question, as <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>) might signify: to get feathers, <hi type="italic">plumescere</hi> (Targ., Jer.), but that gives a tame question; wherefore Gregory understands the <hi type="italic">plumescit</hi> of the Vulgate of moulting, for which purpose the hawk seeks the sunny side. But האביר alone, by itself, cannot signify “to get new feathers;” moreover, an annual moulting is common to all birds, and prominence is alone given to the new feathering of the eagle in the Old Testament, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>; Mic 1:16, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference> (lxx πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί).<note placement="foot">Less unfavourable to this rendering is the following, that אברה signifies the long feathers, and אבר the wing that is composed of them (perhaps, since the Talm. אברים signifies wings and limbs, <hi type="italic">artus</hi>, from אבר = הבר, Arab. <hi type="italic">hbr</hi>, to divide, furnish with joints), although נוצה (from נצה, to fly) is the more general designation of the feathers of birds.</note> <div eID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> Thus, then, the point of the question will lie in לתימן: the hawk is a bird of passage, God has endowed it with instinct to migrate to the south as the winter season is approaching. <div eID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference> the circle of the native figures taken from animal life, which began with the lion, the king of quadrupeds, is now closed with the eagle, the king of birds. It is called נשׁר, from נשׁר, Arab. <hi type="italic">nsr , vellere;</hi> as also <hi type="italic">vultur</hi> (by virtue of a strong power of assimilation = <hi type="italic">vultor</hi>) is derived from <hi type="italic">vellere</hi>, - a common name of the golden eagle, the lamb’s vulture, the carrion-kite (<hi type="italic">Cathartes percnopterus</hi>), and indeed also of other kinds of kites and falcons. There is nothing to prevent our understanding the eagle κατ ̓ εξοχήν, viz., the golden eagle (<hi type="italic">Aquila chrysaëtos</hi>), in the present passage; for even to this, corpses, though not already putrified, are a welcome prey. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference></hi> we must translate either: and is it at thy command that ... ? or: is it so that (as in הכי) at thy command ... ? The former is more natural here. מצוּדה, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.28">Job 39:28</reference></hi>, signifies prop. <hi type="italic">specula</hi> (from צוּד, to spy); then, however, as Arab. <hi type="italic">masâd</hi> (referred by the original lexicons to <hi type="italic">masada</hi>), the high hill, and the mountain-top. The rare form יעלעוּ, for which Ges., Olsh., and others wish to read לעלעוּ or ילעלעוּ (from לוּע, <hi type="italic">deglutire</hi>), is to be derived from עלע, a likewise secondary form out of עלעל (from עוּל, to suck, to give suck), (Note: The Arab. <hi type="italic">‛alla</hi> does not belong here: it gains the signification <hi type="italic">iterum bibere</hi> from the primary signification of “coming over or upon anything,” which branches out in various ways: to take a second, third, etc., drink after the first. More on this point on Isa 3:4. <div eID="gen8706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> Supplementary note: The quadriliteral עלעל to be supposed, is not to be derived from עלל, and is not, as it recently has been, to be compared with Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ll ,</hi> “to drink.” This Arab. verb does not signify “to drink” at all, but, among many other branchings out of its general primary signification, related to עלה, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛lâ</hi>, also signifies: “to take a second, third, etc., drink after the first,” concerning which more details will be given elsewhere. עלעל goes back to עוּל, <hi type="italic">lactare</hi>, with the middle vowel, whence also עויל, <reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.18">Job 12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.11">Job 21:11</reference> (which see). The Hauran dialect has <hi type="italic">‛âlûl</hi> (plur. <hi type="italic">‛awâlı̂l</hi>), like the Hebr. עולל (עולל = מעולל), in the signification <hi type="italic">juvenis</hi>, and especially <hi type="italic">juvencus</hi> (comp. <hi type="italic">infra</hi>, p. 689, note 3, “but they are heifers,” Arab. <hi type="italic">illâ ‛awâlı̂l</hi>).) like שׁרשׁ out of שׁרשׁר (from שׁרר, Arab. <hi type="italic">srr ,</hi> to make firm), Ew. §118, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, comp. Fürst, <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch, sub</hi> עוּל, since instances are wanting in favour of עלע being formed out of לעלע (<hi type="italic">Jesurun</hi>, p. 164). Schult. not inappropriately compares even גלג = גלגל in גּלגּתא, Γολγοθᾶ = גּלגּלתּא. The concluding words, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job 39:30</reference></hi>, are perhaps echoed in Mat 24:28. High up on a mountain-peak the eagle builds its eyrie, and God has given it a remarkably sharp vision, to see far into the depth below the food that is there for it and its young ones. Not merely from the valley in the neighbourhood of its eyrie, but often from distant plains, which lie deep below on the other side of the mountain range, it seizes its prey, and rises with it even to the clouds, and bears it home to its nest.<note placement="foot">Vid., the beautiful description in Charles Boner’s <hi type="italic">Forest Creatures</hi>, 1861.</note> <div eID="gen8707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8708" type="x-p"/> Thus does God work exceeding strangely, but wonderously, apparently by contradictions, but in truth most harmoniously and wisely, in the natural world.  <chapter eID="Job.39"/> <div eID="gen8708" type="x-p"/>

Surely no. And if thou canst not rule such a Creature as this, much less art thou able to govern the World or to teach me how to govern it, which thou presumest to do.</ns0:note>? <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>x</ns0:hi> It is much disputed among the Learned, but is not needful to be known by others, whether there be or ever was such a Creature as we call the Unicorn, or whether this <ns0:hi>Reem,</ns0:hi> which is the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew name of it, be the <ns0:hi>Rhinoceros,</ns0:hi> as some would have it; or a certain kind of wild Goat called <ns0:hi>Onyx,</ns0:hi> which is very tall and strong and untractable; or one of that kind of wild Oxen or Bulls called <ns0:hi>Uri;</ns0:hi> which may seem most probable both from the descrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of this Creature here and elsewhere in Scripture which exactly agrees with its description given by other Authours; and from the de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scription of his work in this place; which must in all reason be agree<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able to Creatures of that general kind; and from the conjunction of this Creature with Bullocks in Scripture, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 17. and espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 34. 6, 7 where having put <ns0:hi>Lambs<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Goats,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rams</ns0:hi> toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. as Creatures of the same or very like sort; he mentions <ns0:hi>Bul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />locks,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bulls</ns0:hi> & <ns0:hi>Reems, v.</ns0:hi> 7. as belonging to the same general sort of Creatures. But this I shall not positively determin here He that would know more may see what the Reverend and Learned Mr. <ns0:hi>Caryl</ns0:hi> hath upon this Text out of <ns0:hi>Bootius</ns0:hi> and others, and my Latin <ns0:hi>Synopsis</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 23. 22.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Canst thou bind the Unicorn with his band in the furrow <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In thy furrowed Field, by a Metonymy. Or, <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> (as the prefix <ns0:hi>Beth</ns0:hi> is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 4. <ns0:hi>Levit</ns0:hi> 16. 22. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 24. 5.) the furrow, i. e. to make Furrows, or to Plow: for which work Cattle use to be bound together that they may be directed by the Husbandman, and may make right Furrows.</ns0:note>? or will he harrow the valleys <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To wit, the low grounds; which are most proper for, and most imployed in the work of Plowing.</ns0:note> after thee <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Under thy conduct following thee step by step.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. Wilt thou trust him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To wit, for the doing of these works?</ns0:note> because his strength is great <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Because he is very able for thy work. And wilt thou by thy power make him wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling or force him to put forth and spend his strength in thy service?</ns0:note>? or wilt thou leave thy labour <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. thy work of Plowing and Harrowing. Or rather 2. the Fruit of thy labour, or the goods gotten by thy labour, as this word is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 33. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 20. 18. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 78. 46 & 128. 2. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 4. 38. to wit, the Fruits of the Earth procured by God's bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing upon thy industry.</ns0:note> to him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To be brought home by him into thy Barns, as the next Verse explains it.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. Wilt thou believe him that he will bring home thy seed <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>will return thy seed;</ns0:hi> either 1. by Plowing and Harrow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing thy Land so well that it shall make a good return to thee for thy seed. Or rather 2. by bringing into thy Barn, as it follows, thy seed, i. e. the product of thy seed, or thy sheaves of Corn, as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Hagg.</ns0:hi> 2. 19.</ns0:note>, and gather <ns0:hi>it into</ns0:hi> thy Barn?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:421" />13. <ns0:hi>Gavest thou</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Stile of this Book is very concise and some Verb is mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />festly wanting to supply the sense; and this seems to be fitly un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood out of <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. where it is expressed.</ns0:note> the goodly <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>triumphant,</ns0:hi> that wherein it triumpheth or prideth it self.</ns0:note> wings <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>feathers.</ns0:hi> Heb. <ns0:hi>wing</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>feather.</ns0:hi> The Peacocks, beauty lies in its tail; which may well enough be comprehended under this Name, as it is confessed that the Latin word <ns0:hi>Ala,</ns0:hi> which properly signifies a <ns0:hi>wing,</ns0:hi> is used by <ns0:hi>Martial</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Claudian</ns0:hi> to express the Peacoks tail.</ns0:note> unto the Peacoks <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, as some render it, <ns0:hi>to the Ostrich:</ns0:hi> whose wings are much more great and goodly than those of the Peacock. And for the other word in the next Clause which is rendred <ns0:hi>Ostrich,</ns0:hi> they translate it another way. For that the Hebrew word <ns0:hi>Hasidah</ns0:hi> doth not signifie <ns0:hi>an Ostrich,</ns0:hi> seems plain from the mention and description of that Bird, <ns0:hi>Psal</ns0:hi> 104. 17. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 8. 7. <ns0:hi>Lament.</ns0:hi> 4. 3. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 5. 9. which doth not at all agree to the Ostrich. And forasmuch as the following Verses do evidently speak of the Ostrich, and it is absurd to discourse of a Bird which had not been so much as named, and consequently the name of it must be found in this Verse, and there is no other word in this Verse which bids so fair for it, it may seem probable that this word is not to be rendred <ns0:hi>the Peacock</ns0:hi> (though it be so taken by most) but <ns0:hi>the Ostrich.</ns0:hi> Nor is it likely that both the Peacock and the Ostrich should be crouded together into one Verse: especially when all the following Characters belong onely to the latter of them. Add to this, that it is confessed even by the Hebrew Writers themselves that there is a great uncertainty in the signification of the Names of Birds and Beasts; and therefore it is not strange if ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny Interpreters were mistaken in the signification of this word.</ns0:note>? or <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>the fea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers of the Stork and Ostrich.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> wings and feathers unto the Ostrich <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>or the wings</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>feathers of the Stork</ns0:hi> (or, <ns0:hi>or) the Ostrich?</ns0:hi> Or, didst thou give (which may be repeated out of the former branch) <ns0:hi>the wings and feathers to the Stork?</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>verily</ns0:hi> (the Particle <ns0:hi>im</ns0:hi> being oft used as a note of confirmation, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 59. 16. & 63. 7, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3. 34. & 23. 18.) it hath <ns0:hi>wings and feathers</ns0:hi> like those <ns0:hi>of a Stork;</ns0:hi> for so indeed they are, black and white like them. And this may be noted as a great and a remarkable work of God, that it should really have wings and feathers as other Birds have, and particularly the Stork, who comes nearest to it in bulk and colour, although otherwise by its vast bulk it might seem to be a Beast rather than a Bird, as it is also called by <ns0:hi>Aristotle</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pliny,</ns0:hi> and others.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. Which <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Which Ostrich; whose property this is noted to be by Naturalists. Or, <ns0:hi>But:</ns0:hi> for this unnatural quality is opposed to the goodliness of her wings or feathers.</ns0:note> leaveth her eggs in the earth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">In the place where she lays them: where she leaves them, either 1. from care lest she should crush and break them if her vast body should sit upon them: or rather 2. from forgetfulness, or carelesness, or unnaturalness, or folly; to which it is manifestly ascribed in the following Verses.</ns0:note>, and warmeth them in the dust <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either 1. covering them with sand that they may be warmed and hatched by that together with the heat of the Sun. But this is judged a fabulous report; for the <ns0:hi>Arabians,</ns0:hi> amongst whom this Bird is most frequent and best known, affirm that such Eggs do quickly perish and putrefie. Or rather 2. exposing them to the heat of the Sun, which being excessive in those hot Countreys, doth and must needs quickly destroy or spoil them. And the Ostrich is said to warm them, because her leaving them there is not onely the occasion, but in some sort the cause of the Suns warming them.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. And forgetteth that the foot <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, of wild Beasts (as it follows) passing that way.</ns0:note> may crush them, or that the wild beast may break them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. She is hardned <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>He,</ns0:hi> i. e. God, <ns0:hi>hardens her.</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>she hardneth her self.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> against her young ones <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Against her eggs, which he calls her <ns0:hi>young ones</ns0:hi> emphatically, to ag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gravate her fault and folly in destroying those Eggs, which, if not neglected, would have been young ones.</ns0:note>, as though <ns0:hi>they were</ns0:hi> not hers <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">As if they were laid by some other Bird. Or, <ns0:hi>that they may not be to her,</ns0:hi> i. e. that they may be utterly lost and destroyed; or as if it were her design to destroy their very being.</ns0:note>: her labour <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To wit, in laying her Eggs is wholly lost.</ns0:note> is in vain without fear <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This may be added as a further aggravation. She doth this, not because she is com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pelled to forsake her Eggs for fear of men or beasts, but meerly out of an unnatural carelesness. Or, she is <ns0:hi>without fear,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>for want of fear,</ns0:hi> to wit, of a provident fear and care about them.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther hath he imparted to her understanding <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Because God hath not implanted in her that natural instinct and providence and affection which he hath put into other Birds and Beasts towards their young. And yet no man presumes to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proach me for making this difference in my Creatures. And as little reason hast thou to blame me for afflicting thee, when others not so bad as thou for the present go unpunished: because I have no less authority over thee, than over them, and can dispose of all my Creatures according to my good pleasure. The great folly of this Bird is noted by <ns0:hi>Arabick</ns0:hi> Writers who best know her, and that not onely for this property of forsaking her own Eggs, but also for other things, as that she eats any thing which is offered to her, as Iron, Stones, Glass, hot Coals, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Whereas other Birds and Beasts have so much sagacity as to reject improper and unwholsome things; that being pursued by the hunter she thinks her self safe and unseen by hiding her head in the Sand: For which and other such qualities it is a Proverb among the <ns0:hi>Arabians, More foolish than an Ostrich.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. What time she lifteth up her self on high <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To flee from her pursuer: to which end she lifteth up her head and body, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ads her wings.</ns0:note>, she scorneth the horse and his rider <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">She despiseth them in regard of her greater swiftness; for though she cannot flie because of her great bulk, being said to be as big as a new-born Camel, yet by the aid of her wings she runs so fast that Horsemen cannot reach her, as both Greek and other Authors have noted.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. Hast thou given the horse strength <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either strength of body: or rather courage and generous confidence, for which the Horse is highly commended.</ns0:note>? hast thou clothed his neck with thunder <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> With snorting and neighing; in the making of which found the Neck, in regard of the Throat which is within it, and a part of it, is a principal instrument: which noise may not unfitly be called <ns0:hi>thunder,</ns0:hi> because of the great vehemency, and rage wherewith it is attended, and the great terrour which it causeth, especially in War and Battel, of which see <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 8. 16. and compare 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 12. 17, 18. where this very term of <ns0:hi>thundring</ns0:hi> is ascribed to a far lower and less terrible noise. Nor is this, as some alledge, an improper speech, because this thunder or neighing is rather clothed with the Neck, as being within it, than the Neck with it; for nothing is more common in Scripture than to say that men are clothed <ns0:hi>with righteousness, humility,</ns0:hi> and other graces, which yet are in strictness of speech within the man, and not he within them. But because this word, in this form, is not elsewhere extant, some render it other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise, <ns0:hi>with a mane,</ns0:hi> with a thick, and full, and deep mane, as the phrase of being clothed with it implies. For this is mentioned by all Writers of Horses, as a notable mark of a generous Horse; which therefore they conceive would not be omitted here where so many several properties and excellencies are described. And the Verb <ns0:hi>Raam,</ns0:hi> whence this comes, in the Syriack Language signifies not onely <ns0:hi>to thunder,</ns0:hi> but also <ns0:hi>to be high</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>lofty:</ns0:hi> which fitly agrees to the mane which is in the highest part of the Horse.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Canst thou make him afraid as a grashopper <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which is easily affrighted and chased away by the least noise of a Man. Or, as divers others render the place, <ns0:hi>didst thou make him to move like a Grashopper,</ns0:hi> skipping and leaping as he goes! So he describes the posture of a gallant and generous Horse, who carvets and praunseth, and as it were danceth as he walks.</ns0:note>? the glory of his nostrils <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That snoring, or sound, and smoke which cometh out of his Nostrils, especially when he is inraged and ingaged in battle, which is another note of a ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerous Horse, and strikes a terrour into his adversary. Or <ns0:hi>the ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hemency,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>majesty,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>magnificence of his snorting,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>snoring</ns0:hi> as this word is rendered, <ns0:hi>Ier<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> 8. 16.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi>
