                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> terrible.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> see<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>dig.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> He paweth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>He diggeth.</ns0:hi> Through courage and wantonness he cannot stand still, but is beating, as it were, digging up the Earth with his feet.</ns0:note> in the valley <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This he adds partly because the ground being there more plain and smooth, he hath the better conveniency for his praunsing and pawing with his feet, which in hilly and uneven ground he cannot so well do, and partly because Battels use to be pitched in Valleys or low grounds, especially Horse Battels</ns0:note>, and rejoyceth in <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> strength <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Making semblance of great pride and complacency in it.</ns0:note>: he goeth on to meet <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the Armour.</ns0:note> the armed men <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">With great readiness and undaunted courage.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. He mocketh at fear <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> At all Instruments and objects of terrour, as <ns0:hi>Fear</ns0:hi> is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 26. & 10. 24. He despiseth what other Creatures dread.</ns0:note>, and is not affrighted: neither turneth he back from the Sword <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>because of the Sword:</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>for fear of the Sword,</ns0:hi> as this phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 21. 15. & 31. 8. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 14. 16. & 50. 16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. The quiver <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, although <ns0:hi>the Quiver,</ns0:hi> &c. So this comes in as an aggra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation of his courage notwithstanding the just causes of fear which are mentioned in this Verse. And <ns0:hi>the Quiver</ns0:hi> is here put for the Arrows contained in it by a Metonymy very usu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al in this very case and in all sorts of Authors, which being shot against the Horse and Rider make this rateling noise here mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:note> rattleth against him, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in flame of the Spear.</ns0:note> the glit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tering spear and the Shield <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or rather the <ns0:hi>Launce</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iavelin.</ns0:hi> For that this was not a defensive, but an offensive weapon seems plain both from this place where it is mentioned among such, and as an object of fear, which the Shield is not, and from <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 8. 18. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 17. 45. where it is so used.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:421" />24. He swalloweth the ground <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The sense is either 1. He is so earnest and eager upon the Battle that he rusheth into it with all speed, and runs over the ground so swiftly, that he might seem to have swallowed it up. Or, 2. He is so full of warlike Rage and Fury, that he not only champs his Bridle, but is ready to tear and devour the very ground on which he goes. And the Phrase here used is not unusual, both in Arabick, and in other Authors: of which see my Latin Synopsis on this place.</ns0:note> with fierceness and rage: neither believeth he that <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> the sound of the trumpet <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He is so pleased with the approach of the Battle, and the sound of the Trumpet calling to it, that he could scarce believe his Ears for gladness. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 45. 26. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 24. 41. Or thus, <ns0:hi>He cannot stand still,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>firm</ns0:hi> (as this Verb and the derivative from it is used, not only in the Chaldee and Syriack Dia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect, but also in the Hebrew, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 59. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 35.) <ns0:hi>when the Trumpet soundeth:</ns0:hi> His Rider can hardly keep him still, but he strives and longs to run to the fight.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25. He saith among the trumpets, ha, ha <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">An Expression of Joy and Alacrity, declared by his proud neighings, whereby he doth in some sort answer the sound of the Trumpets, in way of scorn and challenge.</ns0:note>; and he smelleth <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He perceiveth, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 16. 19.</ns0:note> the battle afar off <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">At some distance, either of place, or rather of time, as the word is most frequently used. He perceives by the motion of the Souldiers, and the clattering of the Arms, that the Battle is at hand, which is very welcome to him.</ns0:note>, the thunder of the cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">By which he understands either the military Orations which the Captains make and deliver with a loud voice to animate their Soul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diers to the Battle: Or rather, the loud and joyful clamour begun by the Commanders, and followed by the Souldiers when they are ready to join Battle, that thereby they may both daunt their Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies, and encourage themselves.</ns0:note>, and the shouting.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. Doth the hawk flie <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">In so singular a manner, so strongly and steddily, so constant<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly and unweariedly, so swiftly and speedily, so regularly and cun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ningly to catch her Prey.</ns0:note> by thy wisdom <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Didst thou inspire her with that Wis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom?</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> stretch her wings toward the south <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which she doth either 1. when she casts her old Feathers, and gets new ones, which is furthered either by the warmth of Southerly Winds, or by the heat of the Sun, which was South<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward from <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s Country, as it is from ours. Whence it is, that as wild Hawks do this by natural Instinct, so the places which Men build for the keeping of tame Hawks are built towards the South. Or in, or towards Winter, when wild Hawks flie into warmer Countries, as being impatient of cold weather.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27. Doth the Eagle mount up <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Flies directly upward till she be out of thy sight; which no o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Bird can do.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:p n="28">28. She dwelleth and abideth upon the rock, upon the crag of the rock <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which she doth, partly for the security of her self and her Young: and partly that she may thence have the better prospect to discern her Prey, as it followeth.</ns0:note>, and the strong place.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29. From thence she seeketh the prey, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> her eyes behold afar off <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Her sight is exceeding sharp and strong, so that she is able to look upon the Sun with open Eyes, and to behold the smallest prey upon the Earth or Sea, when she is mounted out of our sight; which when she spies, she flies to it, with incredible swiftness, e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven like an Arrow out of a Bow.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
